articles.title: The Mecca Pact: A New Treaty Organization, Just Like the Old One
articles.full_text:
MJDA is much like the Cold War’s CENTO and is likely to be just as impactful.
Much has been made of the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement (MJDA) – a collective security agreement signed by Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, and Turkiye in early August – in news and analysis recently. Some have likened this to the Russia-dominated Collective Security Treaty Organization (CSTO). Others have called this a signal of the end of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) and the birth of a new regional order. Though, perhaps reports of NATO’s death are greatly exaggerated. 
And with the benefit of a longer historical lens, we can see how prognostications that MJDA will remake the region’s  security are fairly off the mark. More than anything, MJDA resembles the failed and somewhat forgotten Central Treaty Organization (CENTO) of the Cold War. And, we can expect that, like CENTO, the member states themselves, and those around them, will continue their defense and security planning much as they have before. MJDA is unlikely to solve the problems it purports to confront and will accomplish little more than the Cold War’s CENTO. For a closer modern analogue, perhaps look to the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) structure, a forum for warm promises and suppressed disgruntlement.
But for a moment, let’s turn back the clock. CENTO was launched as the Baghdad Pact in 1955, a defensive agreement between Iran, Iraq, Pakistan, Turkiye (then spelled Turkey), and the United Kingdom, with the United States initially serving as an observer. This was a reaction to the failing World War II global alliance system and the emergence of new security challenges – specifically, the split between capitalism and communism. 
Regionally, secular powers in and around the Middle East feared that a reemergent Soviet Union would follow the path of tsarist Russia. They anticipated that a desire for warm-water ports and hydrocarbons (mainly oil at the time) would drive Moscow’s perceived designs on the Mediterranean Sea, the Persian Gulf, and even the Indian Ocean. So, by encouraging this alliance, Washington could extend First World containment well beyond the borders of NATO. This merged policy to theory that was expressed in the “Long Telegram,” providing “strong resistance” at a possible point where Soviets might probe.
Yet, almost as soon as the ink was dry on the treaty agreement, membership fractured. A military coup overthrew the Iraqi monarch and the country withdrew from the pact in 1958. A Ba’athist revolution shortly thereafter would sever any possible reconciliation with the U.S.-aligned group. And so the group (minus Baghdad) renamed itself CENTO. The alliance didn’t rate very highly years later. In 1963 a cement factory dedication took priority for the Pakistani president, during a summit held in Karachi.
CENTO did have other goals beyond defense. It was supposed to advance economic cooperation and trade, communications, and transportation links between the member states. This included the establishment of a joint nuclear research center in Tehran, supported by London. New communication links were designed with Washington funding construction to better connect Ankara, Tehran, and Karachi; Iran’s Chabahar was envisioned as providing a vital pivot for commerce and movement across the entire region. 
Yet, the central aim of CENTO was mutual defense against Soviet aggression. What did the pact provide for? In short, very little. The defense articles urged mutual cooperation, non-interference in internal affairs, and respect for pre-existing obligations, while leaving open the possibility of accession by other Arab League members. Spoiler: none joined. Only in bilateral deals did the treaty have teeth. Ultimately, the United States took on responsibility to resist outside aggression and provide military or economic assistance necessary to preserve member states’ independence.  
That didn’t really pan out as members looked to their own defense policies. Ultimately, the Soviets didn’t need to force their way through Iran. Moscow established links with Ba’athist governments in CENTO’s “rear,” for example, and built ties in Ethiopia and (then North) Yemen that exploited anti-colonial sentiment. Meanwhile, the United States sanctioned CENTO ally Turkiye in 1974 over the invasion of Cyprus. And in Pakistan’s wars with India, Turkiye and Iran were absent. Indeed, many of the security problems of the 1960s and ’70s that enmeshed CENTO states are still salient today.
All this elides the fact that Soviet leaders Nikita Khrushchev and Leonid Brezhnev had no intention of driving to the sea. The deployment of Soviet forces, regardless of ebbs and flows to U.S.-USSR bilateral relations, was focused on the NATO threat to the west and southwest. Recall, Soviet forces withdrew from Iran shortly after the war ended, and lost their oil concessions as well. The December 1979 invasion of Afghanistan was never predicated on a further push to the Indian Ocean. In sum, the actual security threats facing member states and the political aims of CENTO were misaligned. 
So, how about the MJDA today? The current global context does share some superficial similarities to global politics in the 1950s. As then, today the global order is rapidly transforming. A comfortable modus vivendi between the U.S., Europe, Russia, and China has not yet emerged. And proxy wars at these great powers’ frontiers are challenging the old order that had lasted through most of the Cold War and several decades after.
Yet, as with CENTO, the new MJDA is a treaty without teeth, between states with diverse security problems and little impetus to work together on those challenges. First off, Pakistan, as during CENTO and afterward, remains mired in low-grade conflict with India. India remains the primary threat to Pakistan and the reason that the latter has long sought strategic “depth” in Afghanistan. 
Second, Turkiye, despite trending to strongman governance and fickle defense policies that saw it purchase, then resell, S-400s from Russia, remains the largest ground force in NATO (on the continent). Indeed, Riyadh has little to offer Ankara in terms of conventional capabilities. And fighting around the Straits of Bab el-Mandeb or Hormuz has little impact on Turkiye’s energy revenues. The Baku-Tbilisi-Ceyhan Pipeline’s exports are healthy amid two ongoing wars in the Persian Gulf and eastern Europe.
Third, Saudi Arabia’s regional adventurism is not something that Pakistan or Turkiye are likely to back. Riyadh has the mistaken impression that expensive kit equals a capable military. But repeated aerial bombing of Houthi rebels has done little to turn the tide of that conflict. Pan-Arabism was watery mortar for CENTO and pan-Islamism is likely to prove just as undependable for MJDA.
Another key point: Pakistan and Turkiye already enjoy their own nuclear umbrellas. Pakistan’s survival is guaranteed by its nuclear force of some couple hundred nuclear warheads. Turkiye’s survival is guaranteed by NATO’s nuclear umbrella. Saudi Arabia is the odd partner out here – at least until it develops its own domestic program, something the current U.S. administration has promised to help with. 
Finally, what does the treaty itself commit the partners to? The MJDA, at this point, is a series of statements. Those statements claim that the treaty will consider an armed attack against one an attack against all signatories, and further defense cooperation between the signatories will be encouraged. The latter is so much diplomatese and nothing in previous bilateral agreements impeded such cooperation. 
The former commitment lacks credibility. Importantly, who is the enemy here? Iran? India? Israel? Al-Qaida? Islamic State affiliates? None of the participating states will commit their nuclear forces to a poorly defined enemy that the members don’t even share. As for conventional forces, certainly the member states can share what they are learning about air defenses and drone warfare. But will Ankara or Islamabad commit to defending Riyadh’s airspace? 
This commitment is likely to be tested sooner rather than later with the ongoing Iran-U.S. War. And the most likely outcome is stern statements, arms sales, and perhaps joint training events. 
CENTO disappeared because the supposed threat it was designed to confront – Soviet incursion toward southern ports – had to be contained, even though it was illusory and only faintly hinted at by George Kennan. MJDA, if indeed aimed against Iranian “hegemony,” is trying to similarly commit states to a defense that they don’t share and misplaced security perceptions. 
Much like CENTO, MJDA members just don’t share the same security threats nor do they have the will to commit to mutual defense. Today, there’s not even a foreign policy push from a great or super power behind this alliance. Twenty years from now we will probably talk about MJDA just as much Cold Warriors thought about CENTO a generation after it was formed: not much.

articles.title: Learning Chinese Sign Language
articles.full_text:
There are multiple different sign languages – some of which are not easily intelligible to deaf people.
Learning Chinese Sign Language is a bewildering experience. To begin with, Chinese Sign Language (CSL) is in itself best understood as an umbrella term rather than a well-defined language. 
You have Signed Chinese, shoushi hanyu, which is one-to-one transcriptions of the written standard Chinese into signs, replete with interpuncation such as signed question marks. Then there is Natural Sign Language, ziran shouyu, the language that is actually spoken between native deaf signers in China. It has syntax and grammar markedly different from Chinese, makes extensive use of abbreviations and, like all natural sign languages, incorporates facial expressions. 
Besides these, there are yet other types of CSL described in the academic literature, such as Literary Sign Language (wenfa shouyu) and Society Sign Language (shehui shouyu). All the more confusing is how these terms often seem to overlap or even are used interchangeably.
Since 2018, the government has been actively promoting a type of sign language titled Guojia Tongyong Shouyu, sometimes translated into English as Chinese General Sign Language (CGSL). According to the Chinese Ministry of Education, CGSL can be seen as the sign language equivalent to Standard Mandarin. Having moved away from a standard based on spoken or written Chinese, CGSL incorporates elements from the natural sign languages and thus appears to be less alien to native deaf speakers. While this standardized variety has been described by some Chinese academics as a “natural sign language,” it is, however, uncertain if it is viewed as such by deaf Chinese themselves. 
For the prospective learner, there is a surprisingly user-friendly app based on the official CGSL lexicon. There are daily quizzes, signed demonstrations of the words, targeted tests, themed glossaries, and other useful tools for learning. Unfortunately, all of this does not compensate for the staggering lack of lexemes in the dictionary. Basic and commonly used words such as “curious” or “already” are missing. 
Sometimes the all too familiar top-down perspective of Chinese officialdom shines through with its clear political priorities: while there is an entry for “Taiwan Democratic Self-Government League,” the arguably far more useful word “weekend” is not listed. Even more striking is how words pertaining to sexuality or “taboo” body parts are missing altogether. For example, how would a sign language interpreter fare at a client’s gynecologist visit when the CGSL has no official terms for a woman’s genitalia? 
A couple of years ago, I was myself trying to learn Chinese Sign Language. I began by signing up to an online class, taught for free three nights a week. The teacher, however, was of the old-school, pre-CGSL era. Each lesson he stiffly taught us how to sign Chinese words and characters, without any facial cues and without teaching any grammar. Knowing enough about sign language to recognize that this was not the way deaf Chinese actually speak to each other, I quickly abandoned this approach and figured that the best way would be to befriend native speakers and simply learn from them. 
What I had not foreseen was how the natively spoken natural sign languages not only vary from region to region, but seemingly even from speaker to speaker. Without classroom instruction and with different speakers signing in different ways, it soon became hard to know which was the “correct” way to sign. Apparently, I was not the only one with this problem: one of my deaf acquaintances said he would often not understand what other native deaf speakers were saying. 
In fact, not only do deaf Chinese sometimes have a hard time understanding each other, but most of them struggle to understand the sign language used in official Chinese media. In one study exploring this issue, up to 84 percent of the deaf participants reported having trouble understanding the signed Chinese in television programs. 
Phenomena such as these – official use of sign language that is unintelligible for actual deaf persons – might, in some part, be ascribed to what in Chinese is called xingshi zhuyi, or pointless formalism. The 2008 Law of the People’s Republic of China on the Protection of Disabled Persons stated that there should be sign language available for television shows, and state-owned broadcasting companies might simply want to check that box – without bothering to produce content that is relevant for or even comprehensible to a deaf audience. 
With this said, there is an apparent growing interest among Chinese academics, and clear signs of growing awareness of sign language issues in Chinese society in general. My experiences with learning Chinese Sign Language might already be outdated. In 2023, a long article with the title “The Sign Language Used by Interpreters Is 90 Percent Incomprehensible to Deaf People” ran in the well-renowned Shanghai-based publication The Paper. According to state media, a national standard for proficiency and testing in CGSL has been implemented since March last year. Things are looking up. 
Some of the most exciting developments, however, are taking place on social media. On platforms such as WeChat and Xiaohongshu (RedNote), there are countless content creators discussing the differences between different types of sign language, teaching sign language to others, or poking fun at the stiff, unnatural mimicry of hearing learners. 
Surprisingly enough, some deaf users are also openly discussing governmental policies, seizing a rare opportunity for a marginalized group to talk about the political reforms directly affecting them. That these topics apparently have a low level of political sensitivity might, however, not be something to view entirely as a positive. Perhaps it simply speaks to the level of neglect of the deaf community. 
Nevertheless, the days of “Signed Chinese” seem to be numbered, and younger generations of media-savvy deaf Chinese might quickly become a force to be reckoned with. One could venture to say that the future is looking bright for new learners of Chinese Sign Language. 
Learning Chinese Sign Language is a bewildering experience. To begin with, Chinese Sign Language (CSL) is in itself best understood as an umbrella term rather than a well-defined language.

Then there is Natural Sign Language, ziran shouyu, the language that is actually spoken between native deaf signers in China. It has syntax and grammar markedly different from Chinese, makes extensive use of abbreviations and, like all natural sign languages, incorporates facial expressions. 
Besides these, there are yet other types of CSL described in the academic literature, such as Literary Sign Language (wenfa shouyu) and Society Sign Language (shehui shouyu). All the more confusing is how these terms often seem to overlap or even are used interchangeably.

According to the Chinese Ministry of Education, CGSL can be seen as the sign language equivalent to Standard Mandarin. While this standardized variety has been described by some Chinese academics as a “natural sign language,” it is, however, uncertain if it is viewed as such by deaf Chinese themselves. 
For the prospective learner, there is a surprisingly user-friendly app based on the official CGSL lexicon. There are daily quizzes, signed demonstrations of the words, targeted tests, themed glossaries, and other useful tools for learning. Unfortunately, all of this does not compensate for the staggering lack of lexemes in the dictionary. Basic and commonly used words such as “curious” or “already” are missing. 
Sometimes the all too familiar top-down perspective of Chinese officialdom shines through with its clear political priorities: while there is an entry for “Taiwan Democratic Self-Government League,” the arguably far more useful word “weekend” is not listed. Even more striking is how words pertaining to sexuality or “taboo” body parts are missing altogether. For example, how would a sign language interpreter fare at a client’s gynecologist visit when the CGSL has no official terms for a woman’s genitalia?

The teacher, however, was of the old-school, pre-CGSL era. Each lesson he stiffly taught us how to sign Chinese words and characters, without any facial cues and without teaching any grammar. Knowing enough about sign language to recognize that this was not the way deaf Chinese actually speak to each other, I quickly abandoned this approach and figured that the best way would be to befriend native speakers and simply learn from them. 
What I had not foreseen was how the natively spoken natural sign languages not only vary from region to region, but seemingly even from speaker to speaker. Without classroom instruction and with different speakers signing in different ways, it soon became hard to know which was the “correct” way to sign. Apparently, I was not the only one with this problem: one of my deaf acquaintances said he would often not understand what other native deaf speakers were saying.

articles.title: Bangladesh and the Perils of Pax Silica
articles.full_text:
It could end up exchanging strategic flexibility for an upgraded version of the subcontracting economy it is trying to escape.
U.S. Special Envoy for South and Central Asia Sergio Gor with Bangladesh’s Prime Minister Tarique Rahman at a meeting in Dhaka, Bangladesh, August 1, 2026.
On August 1, U.S. Special Envoy for South and Central Asia Sergio Gor presented a consequential proposition to Bangladesh’s Prime Minister Tarique Rahman to join Pax Silica. “The country has significant potential to become a partner in the global economic security alliance focused on artificial intelligence, semiconductors and critical mineral supply chains,” he said.
On the same day, Dhaka announced that it would join the Shanghai-based World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization (WAICO), initially as an observer. Bangladesh therefore found itself courted by two emerging technology orders in a single news cycle. The invitation deserves neither reflexive rejection nor diplomatic applause. It demands a national strategy. What, then, should Bangladesh do?
Pax Silica was launched in Washington in December 2025 with seven declaration signatories to “build a secure, prosperous, and innovation-driven silicon supply chain — from critical minerals and energy inputs to advanced manufacturing, semiconductors, AI infrastructure and logistics.” By mid-August 2026, 25 countries, including the U.S., U.K., Japan, Singapore and India, had signed on.
Pax Silica is not simply about chips. Its ambition covers the full artificial intelligence stack: minerals, refining, electricity, data infrastructure, semiconductor design and production, logistics, advanced manufacturing, models, and digital platforms. The State Department describes the goal as reducing coercive dependencies and creating trusted supply chains.
The geopolitical interest is equally clear. It seeks to reorganize strategic technology networks to reduce dependence on China. The initiative has already moved beyond diplomatic language. Washington announced a $250 million Pax Silica Fund for mineral processing, infrastructure, and manufacturing. It has supported plans for a 4,000-acre economic security zone in the Philippines, launched a $1.5 billion artificial intelligence investment platform with Southeast Asia, and partnered with Stanford University on an advanced manufacturing curriculum for participating economies. For allied countries, the promise is access to capital, skills, technology networks, trusted markets, and greater protection from supply disruptions.
China’s response has taken both institutional and commercial form. Beijing continues to criticize exclusive blocs and defends open supply chains, while retaining powerful leverage through its dominance of critical mineral processing and selective export controls. It has also backed the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization (WAICO), which presents itself as a development-focused and more inclusive alternative.
Pax Silica may not name China, but the rivalry is no longer implicit. Washington is increasingly asking partners to align their technology ecosystems with one side or the other.
Bangladesh has reasons to explore the offer. Its economy was worth about $456 billion in 2025, and its large domestic market gives it commercial weight. Bangladesh has about 700 chip designers, more than 20,000 annual graduates in computer science and electrical engineering, and a small semiconductor design services industry earning roughly $8 million a year. The government created a national semiconductor task force in 2025, with design, verification, testing, and packaging identified as realistic entry points.
Pax Silica appears to offer Bangladesh a chance to move beyond its garment-dominated export economy by linking local firms and universities with partners in the U.S., Japan, South Korea, India, Singapore, and Europe. Benefits include training, joint research, cybersecurity standards, and cleaner energy finance. Rather than aiming for advanced fabrication, Bangladesh could focus on chip design, testing, packaging, and AI applications. Its Bay of Bengal location, ports, and workforce could provide geostrategic leverage, reducing vulnerability and increasing bargaining power.
However, strategic location is not readiness. Bangladesh’s current capabilities remain far below the level required to bargain as an equal partner. Semiconductor exports of $8 million are tiny beside the announced $1 billion target for 2030. Reliable, affordable electricity remains a national challenge. During the 2026 energy crisis, the government even closed universities early to conserve power. Advanced electronics and data infrastructure require uninterrupted electricity, clean water, specialized chemicals, strong intellectual property rules, cybersecurity, rapid customs clearance, and credible environmental regulation.
The Philippines demonstrates why readiness must come before ambition. Manila joined Pax Silica in April and announced a 4,000-acre hub in New Clark City. The project soon faced demands for Senate scrutiny and public consultation, along with criticism from scientists, farmers, environmental groups, and Indigenous communities. Estimates circulated in the Philippine policy debate suggested that the hub could eventually require 3 gigawatts of electricity and about 130 million liters of water a day.
Concerns also arose over land rights, long leases, waste, transparency, and the distribution of benefits. President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. publicly defended the project. The lesson is not that the Philippine project will fail. It is that a technology coalition cannot substitute for domestic state capacity. Announcing a hub before establishing its energy, water, legal, environmental, and social foundations turns an economic opportunity into a political backlash. Bangladesh should absorb that warning, given its own fragile utilities and limited research capacity.
There is a second danger. Bangladesh could enter Pax Silica not as a technology partner but as a low-cost labor and land platform. Multinational firms might place assembly, testing, or support services in the country while keeping design authority, patents, procurement, and profits abroad. World Bank research on global value chains shows that technology spillovers depend on the absorptive capacity of local firms, supplier linkages, skills, and deliberate policy. Foreign investment alone does not guarantee industrial upgrading.
Alliance theory warns that Bangladesh risks trading autonomy for limited benefits in Pax Silica. Morrow’s asymmetric alliance model shows weaker states often concede policy freedom, while Keohane’s reciprocity norm stresses mutual gains. Bangladesh currently offers geography and labor but little scarce technology, weakening its bargaining power. True readiness, including local research, training, and supplier development, is essential for negotiating durable, reciprocal partnerships.
Bangladesh has long sought strategic autonomy. Pax Silica is not a military treaty, but its trusted-technology logic can carry demands on vendors, export controls, data governance, critical minerals, telecommunications, and relations with Chinese firms. Recent reporting suggests that Washington increasingly expects partners to choose sides in the artificial intelligence contest.
For Bangladesh, the China question is unavoidable. In the 2024 to 2025 fiscal year, Bangladesh imported $20.61 billion in goods from China, equal to about 30.6 percent of all goods imports. Chinese companies and finance are deeply embedded in power, transport, telecommunications, and industrial supply. Bangladesh also joined China’s new artificial intelligence organization as an observer on the very day Gor raised Pax Silica. Full participation in both systems may be possible while commitments remain loose, but that space could narrow as standards and security rules harden.
The same dangers apply if Bangladesh joins the Chinese camp. WAICO could pressure Dhaka to adopt Chinese vendors, standards, and data rules, leaving Bangladesh with little bargaining power. Since Chinese firms already dominate its power, transport, and telecom sectors, deeper alignment risks greater dependency. It could also reduce Western access to capital and markets. The real issue is Bangladesh’s weak technological base, which makes it vulnerable whichever side it chooses.
Bangladesh should therefore engage, but not accede prematurely. Dhaka’s answer should be neither no nor yes. It should be not yet, and not without a bargain. Pax Silica can become a pathway into the artificial intelligence economy, but only if Bangladesh enters with capabilities that others need and conditions that its citizens can defend. Otherwise, the country may exchange strategic flexibility for an upgraded version of the subcontracting economy it is trying to escape.

articles.title: Namal Rajapaksa’s Arrest and Sri Lanka’s Politics of Mutual Protection
articles.full_text:
The old establishment elites have opposed Namal’s arrest. They want to preserve a system where one of their own is not jailed for corruption.
Sri Lanka Podujana Party parliamentarian Namal Rajapaksa waves to his supporters in the Tissamaharama electorate of Hambantota District, Sri Lanka, Aug. 29, 2026.
Sri Lankan investigators arrested Namal Rajapaksa on September 4 over allegations that he received 100 million Sri Lankan rupees (about $800,000 per 2014-15 exchange rates) in bribes linked to an aircraft procurement deal involving SriLankan Airlines in 2012-13.
The arrest shows that investigators have moved beyond airline officials and business intermediaries to a member of Sri Lanka’s most powerful political family.
The reaction to the arrest was interesting. The United National Party (UNP), which led the 2015-19 Yahapalanaya (good governance) government under which several investigations against Rajapaksa began, joined the Rajapaksa family-led Sri Lanka Podujana Peramuna (SLPP) in condemning his arrest. Their response also demonstrates why a political party from outside the UNP-SLPP establishment needed to be in power to pursue investigations against powerful politicians.
Most of the political opposition and their allies in the media and religious establishments have come out in support of the Rajapaksas, and enormous resources are being spent to discredit the arrest of Namal. Thus, the question is not merely whether Namal will be convicted, but whether the National People’s Power (NPP) anti-corruption campaign can survive contact with the same political pressures that neutered every previous attempt to hold Sri Lanka’s elites to account.
In 2020, Airbus agreed to pay nearly $4 billion to settle international bribery investigations. As part of the investigations, foreign officials traced suspicious payments linked to SriLankan Airlines’ aircraft purchases, and a British court made details of the transactions public. In response, the Gotabaya Rajapaksa government arrested former SriLankan Airlines CEO Kapila Chandrasena and his wife. But the investigation went no further; the two were released on bail, and no action was taken to determine whether Chandrasena and others worked with politicians.
Even in 2020, authorities knew that part of the money had been sent to a company connected to businessman Nimal Perera, who was closely associated with the Rajapaksas. Yet neither the Gotabaya Rajapaksa administration (2019-2022) nor the Ranil Wickremesinghe administration (2022-2024) investigated what Perera did with the money. That investigation was only initiated after the NPP came into power.
The Commission to Investigate Allegations of Bribery or Corruption (CIABOC) told the court that 1.454 million euros (or $1.69 million as per the September 2026 exchange rate) in bribe money was deposited into a Standard Chartered Bank account in Singapore maintained by Biz Solutions Inc., a company registered in Brunei and controlled by Chandrasena’s wife. Of that amount, $800,000 was allegedly transferred to an Oversea-Chinese Banking Corporation Limited (OCBC) account in Singapore maintained by Sabre Vision Holdings Ltd., a company belonging to Perera. Investigators allege that Perera converted the money into Sri Lankan rupees and handed it to Namal Rajapaksa in several installments during 2014 and 2015.
After investigations began under the NPP, investigators traveled to Australia, where Perera now lives, and obtained a sworn affidavit from him. He reportedly refused to return to Sri Lanka because of alleged threats to his life but told investigators that he had handed the rupee equivalent of the $800,000 to Namal Rajapaksa.
Deputy Solicitor General Janaka Bandara also told the court that CIABOC and the Criminal Investigation Department had conducted a joint investigation with assistance from Australia, Singapore, France, and the United States. Airbus officials had also visited the commission several times. An Airbus delegation was in Colombo as recently as August to assist investigators.
These collaborations give the case a stronger foundation. The foreign banking records and international cooperation cannot easily be dismissed as inventions of the NPP. But the most important part of the allegation, i.e., that the money ultimately reached Namal, depends heavily on Perera’s testimony.
President’s Counsel Sampath Mendis, appearing for Namal, argued that neither Airbus officials nor French investigators had accused his client of receiving money. He also questioned Perera’s credibility.
The SLPP had planned a rally under Rajapaksa’s leadership in Anuradhapura on September 12, and the party alleged that the arrest was designed to disrupt its mobilization and weaken its national organizer.
The UNP, which once claimed to be arch-enemies of the Rajapaksas, came to Namal’s aid. It condemned the arrest as an attempt to sabotage the SLPP rally and insisted that Namal had the same democratic right as President Anura Dissanayake to travel around the country and hold public meetings. Wickremesinghe said that with Namal’s arrest, the government was weakening the opposition and threatening Sri Lanka’s democratic system.
The UNP’s response is ironic as investigations into Namal and other members of his family began during the UNP-led Yahapalanaya government. Ever since the Rajapaksas came into power in 2005, the UNP (the main opposition party at the time) insisted that they were a rogue and corrupt political dynasty that is undermining democracy, the rule of law, and the independence of institutions.
When the UNP-led Yahapalanaya administration came to power in 2015, a number of probes were launched against the Rajapaksas. Financial crime investigators arrested Namal twice in 2016 in connection with separate money-laundering allegations. But as with many cases filed during the Yahapalanaya government, these yielded little result and strengthened Rajapaksas’ claims that these lawsuits were examples of political victimization that would not survive judicial scrutiny. The failure of these investigations played a significant role in the return of the Rajapaksas to power in 2019.
Relations between the UNP and the SLPP changed after Sri Lanka’s economic collapse drove Gotabaya Rajapaksa from office in 2022. Wickremesinghe became president through a parliamentary vote and governed with the support of the SLPP majority. Former adversaries became partners in preserving a power structure that had benefitted both sides for decades. The alliance between the two parties validated what the Sri Lankan left had been saying for years — the established political parties are no longer distinguishable from each other and have a vested interest in preserving the status quo. This was another reason for the NPP victory in 2024.
Now in opposition, Wickremesinghe is opposing Namal’s arrest over the Airbus deal. His response is another example of how Sri Lanka’s established political elites close ranks when accountability threatens their power and privilege.
President Dissanayake recently said that Sri Lanka’s former governments had played “cops and robbers” for decades. One group pretended to pursue the other until they exchanged roles. “They were just playing a game,” he said, “but now the real police have arrived.”
Namal Rajapaksa’s arrest is important because the Airbus investigation has now crossed from investigating corporate intermediaries to the political power behind the intermediaries. It also exposes the relationship between two political camps that once pretended to be mortal enemies but now recognize a common threat in the NPP’s accountability campaign.
Sri Lanka’s previous accountability efforts failed because there was no political will on either side to punish powerful politicians.  The Yahapalanaya government’s cases against the Rajapaksas were abandoned not because they could not be proven but because the UNP and the SLPP wanted to preserve a system where former leaders were not jailed for corruption. The difference now is that the NPP has no stake in preserving the old system.

articles.title: Asia’s Economic Integration: A Roadmap for Peacebuilding in the Middle East
articles.full_text:
Economic cooperation in the Asia-Pacific has been the key driver of peace since 1952.
When the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, ASEAN, was formed in 1967, the five founding states intended to produce a front against the spread of communism. The venture has since grown to include a total of 11 countries, producing a remarkable set of unforeseen consequences, from becoming the fifth-largest economy in the world to reinforcing peace across a swath of diverse and developing countries.
Instead of pursuing Cold War initiatives, the bloc has become increasingly integrated, tied together through manufacturing supply chains, trade infrastructure, and shared financial institutions like the Chiang Mai Initiative. ASEAN now produces over $4 trillion in GDP and has a population of 678 million people. The collaboration’s biggest success, however, has not simply been increased commerce. With economic integration comes regional stabilization and peace, a consequence further fostered by the signing of the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP) in 2020, which includes Australia, China, Japan, New Zealand, and South Korea. Economic cooperation in the Asia-Pacific has been the key driver of peace in the region ever since 1952 with the Treaty of San Francisco, and it serves today as a key example of how market mechanics can drive peacebuilding. In fact, it was ASEAN that eroded tensions from the Konfrontasi war in the early 1960s, and has solidified the climate of peace between the Southeast Asian members ever since.
Economists and politicians have often considered the question of whether trade contributes to peaceful relations between states. The affirmative answer is not novel; however, in the case of ASEAN and the Asia-Pacific, the specifics begin to clarify the theory. Peacebuilding through economic means is more a matter of building economic capacity and trade interdependence than of simply trading goods between nations. This crucial specification turns the Asia-Pacific from a successful case study into a model for peacebuilding elsewhere, and it is one that has been imitated by the Gulf Cooperation Council or, more recently, by the C5 in Central Asia.
Economic interdependence is a consequence of cooperation, occurring over time by building trust and relying on companies that diversify operations across countries. Daron Acemoglu, a Nobel Prize winner in Economic Sciences, has regularly argued for this by pointing out that both prosperity and stability mutually flow from systems or institutions that offer a broad stake in the economic growth of a nation. Thus, when firms create cross-border commerce, war becomes economically unviable and politically undesirable. The principle is not exclusive to the Asia-Pacific, and despite ASEAN’s success, it is clear that outliers perpetuate risks by building up economic barriers instead of interdependence. Examples include relations between North and South Korea or China and Taiwan. The question, therefore, remains: how can peace be built today through economic interdependence, or in other words, how can rivals begin working together in an economic capacity?
Answers learned in the Asia-Pacific could resound further away. In the Middle East, for example, diplomatic efforts for peace in Afghanistan, Iraq, Syria, and Israel and the Palestinian Territories have worked through a long campaign of advocacy; however, it is only with the additional incentives that economic cooperation brings that peace efforts actually remain sustainable and enduring. For Israel and the Palestinian Territories, economic interdependence and a shared aspiration could enhance the ongoing international effort to ameliorate decades-long tensions. Syria offers an immediate test case as well. When the Assad regime fell in 2025 and the United States and the European Union both lifted sanctions, organizations began to move in, building relationships and supporting the fragile new state’s desire for peace. American companies have established power generation projects, the Gulf states and Turkey have signed dozens of economic memoranda of understanding with the new state, and startups like Behti Betak or nonprofit organizations like the Words of Isa are building grassroots relationships aimed at creating a newly integrated Syria, driving peace across the Middle East. Integration leads to interdependence. Interdependence self-reinforces peace.
Peacebuilding of this sort may be especially critical for Israel and the Palestinian Territories, where conflict and violence have persisted for decades before the Gaza War. Reconstruction and reconciliation efforts require that businesses spread their operations across the divide. Organizations like the Portland Trust, based in the United Kingdom, have focused on the region on the basis that economic co-operation and dialogue between the parties is inseparable from diplomatic peacebuilding efforts. And such economic development (alongside political will) can create hope, ambition, and opportunities for Palestinians. The founding Chief Executive of The Portland Trust, Lord Jonathan Kestenbaum, brings a personal history to the work of reconciliation. His family’s own flight from Nazi persecution ultimately led them to the UK, where he grew up, and whilst a student in London, he was General Secretary (mazkir) of Bnei Akiva UK, a branch of the global youth movement. He then studied at the Hebrew University in Jerusalem in the 1980s completing an MA in education, and thereafter helped to build an international training program for young educators. As a dual national at the time, Kestenbaum was conscripted to military service, with this experience influencing his life-long commitment to reconciliation between Palestinians and Israelis with a particular focus on building bridges through economic co-operation.
Lord Kestenbaum returned home to the U.K. after a few years in Jerusalem and gave up his dual nationality, retaining only British citizenship. He helped found the Portland Trust, and spent many years fostering peace efforts between Israelis and Palestinians. This history gave him a grounding in the region, a commitment to co-existence and a familiarity that exemplifies how peacebuilding through commerce is not abstract policy but is instead built through relationships and real-life experiences. The Portland Trust has to date worked extensively to support Palestinians and Israelis through projects like the Palestinian Agriculture Impact Fund and the building of the city of Rawabi.
Personal experiences bring markets together, and when they come together, they accelerate growth and integration among an increasing number of actors. Each of these actors learns to empathize with their business partners, regardless of historical or political differences. The process reinforces peace, builds harmony, and creates trust. In the case of Israel and the Palestinian Territories, the process is needed alongside reconstruction efforts like Trump’s Board of Peace, which aims to produce lasting peace but has yet to break ground.
Peace is not guaranteed through economics; however, throughout the last century, and in the case of the Asia-Pacific, it has become the most reliable mechanism of sustaining peace, cultivating the types of relationships that grow closer instead of farther apart. Private investment adds a financial tie to the process; however, intentional relationships with an empathetic desire for peace fundamentally secure the process. Southeast Asia’s history, compared to Syria’s cautious reopening or Gaza’s Board of Peace, shows that commerce can lay groundwork that politics otherwise cannot. The region will need institutional support, perhaps even at the level of an ASEAN, but the foundation is growing. More inter-state commerce will bring stronger relationships, paving the way forward to a future of peace, stability, and economic growth.
When the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, ASEAN, was formed in 1967, the five founding states intended to produce a front against the spread of communism. The venture has since grown to include a total of 11 countries, producing a remarkable set of unforeseen consequences, from becoming the fifth-largest economy in the world to reinforcing peace across a swath of diverse and developing countries.
Instead of pursuing Cold War initiatives, the bloc has become increasingly integrated, tied together through manufacturing supply chains, trade infrastructure, and shared financial institutions like the Chiang Mai Initiative. ASEAN now produces over $4 trillion in GDP and has a population of 678 million people. The collaboration’s biggest success, however, has not simply been increased commerce. With economic integration comes regional stabilization and peace, a consequence further fostered by the signing of the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP) in 2020, which includes Australia, China, Japan, New Zealand, and South Korea. Economic cooperation in the Asia-Pacific has been the key driver of peace in the region ever since 1952 with the Treaty of San Francisco, and it serves today as a key example of how market mechanics can drive peacebuilding. In fact, it was ASEAN that eroded tensions from the Konfrontasi war in the early 1960s, and has solidified the climate of peace between the Southeast Asian members ever since.

The affirmative answer is not novel; however, in the case of ASEAN and the Asia-Pacific, the specifics begin to clarify the theory. Peacebuilding through economic means is more a matter of building economic capacity and trade interdependence than of simply trading goods between nations. This crucial specification turns the Asia-Pacific from a successful case study into a model for peacebuilding elsewhere, and it is one that has been imitated by the Gulf Cooperation Council or, more recently, by the C5 in Central Asia.
Economic interdependence is a consequence of cooperation, occurring over time by building trust and relying on companies that diversify operations across countries. Daron Acemoglu, a Nobel Prize winner in Economic Sciences, has regularly argued for this by pointing out that both prosperity and stability mutually flow from systems or institutions that offer a broad stake in the economic growth of a nation. Thus, when firms create cross-border commerce, war becomes economically unviable and politically undesirable. The principle is not exclusive to the Asia-Pacific, and despite ASEAN’s success, it is clear that outliers perpetuate risks by building up economic barriers instead of interdependence. Examples include relations between North and South Korea or China and Taiwan. articles.title: After the Bangsamoro Poll, Can Politics Maintain the Peace?
articles.full_text:
The peace process in the autonomous region will continue long after the votes have been counted and a new government formed.
The Bangsamoro Transition Authority votes on a proposed transition plan as an interim Bangsamoro Parliament in a special session on June 17, 2019.
On September 14, more than 2.3 million registered voters in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) in the southern Philippines will go to the polls for the first regular parliamentary election.
The immediate priority is that the elections should be peaceful, orderly, and credible, but beyond that there is another question that deserves attention: what will political competition look like in communities where political loyalties are changing, particularly in areas historically aligned with the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF)? The answer could have important consequences for the peace process.
Election-related violence is not new to the Bangsamoro. It long predates the peace agreement with the MILF, and has often been associated with clan rivalries, private armed groups, and local political competition rooted in longstanding disputes. In many communities, elections can even appear relatively peaceful because political power is concentrated within a dominant family or network. The absence of violence, therefore, does not necessarily mean the absence of political contestation; sometimes, it simply reflects the absence of meaningful competition.
As I have argued previously, the movement’s political environment has become increasingly fragmented. Former allies now find themselves competing through different political formations, including the United Bangsamoro Justice Party (UBJP) and the Bangsamoro Federalist Party (BFP). Some may remain aligned with UBJP, while others have moved toward BFP or other competing parties and candidates. This raises the question of whether former allies who once operated within a common political and organizational framework can compete against one another without reproducing the patterns of conflict that the peace process was designed to transform.
There is a danger of interpreting every violent incident during the election period as evidence that the peace process is failing. This would overlook the longstanding nature of election-related violence in the Bangsamoro, which has long existed independently of the Muslim insurgency and the peace process. Thus, reports of localized violence that have appeared in recent weeks and months need to be examined carefully.  The important question here is where these incidents are occurring, who is involved, and whether they are connected to the emerging political dynamics that surround them.
At the same time, assuming that all such incidents are merely ordinary election violence could obscure emerging risks to the peace process. In this case, the important goal is whether local disputes can still be contained through the institutions and relationships established by the process.
The government of the Philippines and MILF have taken steps to maintain a ceasefire during the election period. The security mechanisms established under the peace process have coordinated arrangements for the polls, reflecting the recognition that political competition should not disrupt the cessation of hostilities.
But elections create challenges that cannot always be resolved through ceasefire arrangements alone. The difficulty becomes particularly apparent when communities that were previously aligned around the MILF become politically divided. At the community level, these divisions can cut across families, former comrades, and other longstanding relationships.
This is a normal feature of political transition. Former combatants are expected to become citizens and political actors with different choices and interests. However, it also represents a significant transformation. The peace process once depended in part on the ability of the MILF to maintain organizational cohesion and discipline among its forces and communities. Democratic politics, by contrast, requires the acceptance of political pluralism. Thus, the challenge is to ensure that the shift from political cohesion to political pluralism does not become a transition from one form of conflict to another.
The August 15 ambush of BARMM’s Interim Chief Minister Abdulraof Macacua’s convoy has underscored the uncertainty in the pre-election environment.  The incident has been interpreted in a variety of ways, and there has been speculation on social media that individuals aligned with the BFP may have “staged” it, exposing deepening rifts within the MILF.  The MILF and Philippine government have condemned the incident, and authorities continue to investigate its circumstances. Nevertheless, this episode illustrates that in a fragile political transition, perceptions can themselves become consequential.
For a peace process built on confidence among former adversaries, this is a major concern. While a certain amount of violence may be inevitable, the important variable is whether political actors and communities continue to believe that disputes can be managed through legitimate institutions.
This is why the success of the September 14 elections will likely be gauged after election day. Will losing candidates accept the results? Will political parties trust the electoral institutions? Will communities regard the new parliament as legitimate? And will political disputes remain within the institutional arena, or will they spill into clan networks, armed structures, or other forms of coercion?
A credible election can strengthen these institutions by demonstrating that political authority can be acquired and contested through democratic means. But if political actors perceive the process as unfair, or if communities believe that political competition is being settled through intimidation or violence, distrust could extend beyond individual candidates to the institutions themselves, posing a more serious challenge to the peace process. Thus, the political system that emerges from them should be trusted enough to contain political competition peacefully.
The current fragmentation of the MILF’s political environment could also create opportunities for spoilers. An armed group could take advantage of a clan dispute, for example, or political actors could use a local incident to deepen divisions or challenge the legitimacy of an electoral outcome. A useful post-election assessment should examine whether any violent incidents involve former conflict actors, whether they spread across MILF communities, whether political actors mobilize around them, and whether existing peace mechanisms are able to contain them.
One encouraging development is that the Philippine government and MILF are already looking beyond election day. The joint implementing panels agreed to continue their engagement through a special meeting in Kuala Lumpur on September 25. This is important because whatever the electoral outcome, the peace process will remain unfinished.
If the election produces a result that one faction strongly dislikes, can the Philippine government and MILF still return to the negotiating table, and can disagreements over the emerging political order be managed without suspending cooperation on normalization? These may prove more consequential aspects of their agenda than whether the election itself is entirely free of localized incidents.
The first parliamentary election represents a significant milestone for the Bangsamoro peace process, but its ultimate success will be judged by the character of political competition after the ballots are counted.  The transition requires that, as political actors, former combatants accept that they can lose, that their former allies can become legitimate competitors, and that institutions must provide the arena in which those disagreements are settled.

articles.title: From 9/11 to Pahalgam: India’s Evolving Strategy in the Global War on Terror
articles.full_text:
The September 11 attacks reshaped how the world thinks about – and addresses – terrorism. India is no exception.
Soldiers pose for a photo with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi at Adampur Air Force Base in Punjab on May 13, 2025, following Operation Sindoor.
Some incidents in world history not only leave deep scars on the soul of a nation but alter the nation’s trajectory irreversibly. The terror attack of September 11, 2001 was one such incident. A perfectly normal morning turned into a horrific nightmare when 19 al-Qaida terrorists hijacked four passenger planes, two of which crashed into the Twin Towers in New York and one into the Pentagon building outside of Washington, D.C. The Twin Towers came crashing down and the result was a death count of almost 3,000. 
The resultant national outrage and anger led to the United States leading its most extensive military mission since the Vietnam War, chasing al-Qaida and its leader Osama bin Laden into Afghanistan. In a military campaign lasting almost 20 years, al-Qaida was largely neutralized and Osama bin Laden was eventually tracked and killed in Pakistan on May 2, 2011. 
The 9/11 attacks led to profound changes in the United States as well, especially in matters of internal security. There was a clear mandate that no matter what, there cannot be another 9/11 type of incident on the American mainland ever again.  
In the Indian context however, it took decades of terror attacks before India similarly said, “no more.” Thanks to a policy crafted by Pakistan in the early 1990s to “bleed India through a thousand cuts” with cross-border terrorism, India endured a large number of terror attacks and losses, especially in Kashmir. But then one terror incident shook India like never before.
The terror attack in Pahalgam on April 22, 2025 killed 26 innocent civilians in a popular tourist spot in Kashmir. The attack was launched by terrorists belonging to The Resistance Force, an offshoot of the Pakistan-based Lashkar-e-Taiba (LeT). The anger and outrage in India were magnified many times over as the victims – all men – were specifically identified by their religion (Hindu, except for one Christian and one local Muslim who tried to intervene). The men were also shot dead in front of their wives.  
The resultant military operation, Operation Sindoor, launched by India into Pakistan on May 7, made clear India’s new resolve against terrorism.
While these two incidents – 9/11 and the Pahalgam attack – were separated by almost 24 years, they are united by two nations’ expressed resolve to fight terror to the ends of the Earth. But as the Pahalgam attack sadly showed, the war against terror has not been won. 
Al-Qaida may not be a force to reckon with in the form it was 25 years ago and it may no longer have leaders like Osama bin Laden who could attract and ideologically indoctrinate youth to join. But many smaller offshoots of al-Qaida still operate across the globe. In the Indian context, while LeT and other Pakistan-based terror groups may have been dealt a punishing blow by India, inputs from Pakistan indicate that there is a strong resolve to revive these groups. Therefore, the fight against terror isn’t over yet. 
It is therefore important to examine how terror is changing form and how nations are constantly evolving their strategies to stay ahead of the curve to counter and neutralize such threats before they manifest.
Over the past 25 years, the form terrorism has changed, as have the type of instruments used to carry out terror attacks. Naturally, the strategies to tackle terror have evolved as well. 
Unlike big terror groups like al-Qaida or the Islamic State (IS) in the past, terror groups have now morphed into smaller and more autonomous groups. Lone wolf attacks are now becoming the norm and technologies like drones, cyber, and even artificial intelligence are being used by terror groups. Indirect attacks like cyberattacks on key energy and banking infrastructure are complementing high-impact physical attacks on the population. 
Hierarchical organizations and organized training camps are increasingly giving way to more fluid structures, which operate through affiliations and franchises, encrypted communications, cryptocurrencies, social media, and loosely connected cells. Campaigns seeking territorial control like the IS in Iraq and Syria are being replaced by terror campaigns to disrupt social cohesion within a country and bleed nations financially.
And, accordingly, strategies to fight terror by countries too are evolving rapidly. Counterterrorism has evolved from a predominantly military campaign into a much broader strategy incorporating multiple instruments of state power like intelligence, financial surveillance, border control, cyber monitoring, deradicalization, and international cooperation. When military action is taken, it takes the form of precision operations through cutting-edge standoff weapon platforms.
The fight against terror in India had a frustrating beginning. In most cases, the response to terrorist attacks was limited to sectoral military operations, tightening border controls, and issuing warnings to Pakistan. In some cases, it also led to cutting off diplomatic ties for some time. 
The first such terror attack was the hijacking of Air India’s flight IC-814 on December 24, 1999, just a few months after the Kargil war. With very few options then and increasing public pressure, India agreed to release two Pakistan-based terrorists, Ahmed Omar Shiekh and Masood Azhar, in exchange for over 160 civilian hostages. Massod Azhar went on to establish Jaish-e-Mohammad (JeM), the Pakistan-based terrorist group that later launched a terror attack on the Indian Parliament on December 13, 2001. Caught by surprise, India ordered a full-scale military mobilization under Operation Parakaram, but it ultimately ended without a bullet being fired.
The 26/11 Mumbai terror attack in 2008 was a milestone in many ways. Widely considered as India’s 9/11 moment, it brought global attention to India’s war against terror. Although once again India did not end up punishing Pakistan for the attack, it did lead to a major security review and structural changes. The National Investigative Agency (NIA) was formed as a result, with sweeping powers on matters of internal national security. The NIA is now functioning as the central counterterrorism law enforcement agency in India. 
The mandate of fighting terror expanded to include stronger intelligence coordination, tighter coastal security and border surveillance, specialized forces to fight terror, and cooperation between central and state agencies. The overall responsibility for coastal security was placed under the Indian Navy. 
Tracking and monitoring terror finance too became a key instrument in the fight against terror.  The Multi Agency Center, which was established in December 2001 as a part of the key recommendations of the Kargil Review Committee, also became a key coordination platform for intelligence exchange and cooperation against terror. However, most of India’s anti-terrorism measures remained passive, reactive, and preventive.
It was only after 2014, when the Modi government came to power, that the intent to deliver a decisive response to any act of terror grew firm. Counterterrorism operations in Kashmir were given a new momentum and measures to block infiltration across the Line of Control were strengthened. 
A terror attack on September 18, 2016 by JeM terrorists against an army camp in Uri, Kashmir, led to the first cross-border surgical strikes by the Indian Army, which destroyed multiple terrorist camps and infrastructure in Pakistan. It was not only a strong reply to the terror attack but also signaled a major shift in India’s strategic policy and rules of engagement regarding cross-border terrorism. 
While it did deter Pakistan to some extent, it did not end its terror campaign. On February 14, 2019, JeM terrorists unleashed another terror attack, this time on a police convoy in Pulwama, Kashmir, killing 40 soldiers. Upping the ante, this time, the India Air Force launched strikes on a terror camp of JeM in Balakot, Pakistan on February 26. It was the first time that the Indian Air Force had crossed into Pakistani airspace to launch a strike against terror. 
However, it was the terror attack in Pahalgam on April 22, 2025 that outraged the nation like never before. Modi vowed to track the terrorists “to the ends of the Earth.” With an aim to deliver a decisive blow to the terror network in Pakistan, the Indian Armed Forces launched Operation Sindoor on May 7, hitting the heart of the Pakistan-based terror network. Within 96 hours, nine major terrorist camps destroyed and India had even hit key military assets like airfields and radar stations, forcing Pakistan to seek a ceasefire.
However, the Indian experience tells us that the fight against terror is far from over. With Pakistan unlikely to give up on its policy of state-sponsored terror against India, new forms of threats are likely to emerge. India therefore cannot think that Operation Sindoor is enough to deter any future terror attacks from across the border. In the fight against terror, no deterrence strategy can be absolute. It has to evolve, keeping pace with technology and terror tactics, and hope to stay one step ahead. 
A key to this constantly evolving thought is PRAHAAR, India’s first comprehensive National Counter Terrorism Policy & Strategy which was unveiled on February 23, 2026. This provides a national counterterrorism framework for prevention of, and responding   to terrorist activities and radicalization through coordinated “whole of government” and “whole of society” approaches.
As the world marks the 25 years of the 9/11 attack, the lesson is not whether terror has been defeated but whether nations are equipped well enough to disrupt and deter future terror threats. The success of any strategy is measured by its outcomes. Even if one major terror attack succeeds despite hundreds of potential terror attacks being thwarted, the strategy would still be termed a failure. 
The October 7, 2023 Hamas terror attack into Israel is an example: the best of intelligence and overwhelming military superiority could not preempt or prevent the attack. The events of October 7 not only killed almost 1,200 people in Israel but unleashed a brutal conflict in Gaza and West Asia, which still continues to this day. 
For India, the fight against terror predates 9/11. Over 25 years later, that fight continues, strengthened now with a new political-military resolve and constantly evolving methods of deterrence.
Some incidents in world history not only leave deep scars on the soul of a nation but alter the nation’s trajectory irreversibly. The terror attack of September 11, 2001 was one such incident. A perfectly normal morning turned into a horrific nightmare when 19 al-Qaida terrorists hijacked four passenger planes, two of which crashed into the Twin Towers in New York and one into the Pentagon building outside of Washington, D.C. The Twin Towers came crashing down and the result was a death count of almost 3,000.
articles.summary: The September 11 attacks reshaped how the world thinks about – and addresses – terrorism. India is no exception.

articles.title: From 9/11 to the Iran War, Pakistan-US Ties Remain Transactional
articles.full_text:
There’s a reason the nation’s relationship with the U.S. has fluctuated while India’s has largely held steady.
U.S. President Donald Trump is presented gifts from Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif and Field Marshal Asim Munir in the Oval Office of the White House, Washington D.C., Sep. 25, 2025.
Twenty-five years ago, the September 11 attacks transformed Pakistan’s relationship with the United States. Almost overnight, Pakistan went from facing American sanctions and limited diplomatic attention to becoming a frontline partner in the U.S.-led war in Afghanistan.
In its counterterrorism cooperation, Pakistan offered vital ground-and air-based logistical transit to Afghanistan as well as intelligence and military action. In return, the United States provided financial reimbursement and military assistance in the form of subsidized sale of military hardware and technology. 
The relationship became increasingly strained as the two sides accused each other of failing to deliver what had been promised. Yet the two sides remained close as long as Washington needed Pakistan for the war in Afghanistan.
When the U.S. military withdrew from Afghanistan in August 2021, much of the urgency behind the relationship disappeared. Washington’s political attention declined, although counterterrorism, trade, health, and other forms of engagement continued at the institutional level.
Twenty-five years after 9/11, Pakistan and the United States appear to have entered another period of warm relations. Pakistan has again presented itself as a useful partner through mediation between Washington and Tehran, alongside cryptocurrency deals, critical mineral investments, and counterterrorism cooperation.
As Pakistan mediates in the Iran-U.S. war, given the difficulties of reaching a truce, there’s a constant fear of Pakistani leaders becoming the eventual fall guys. To avert that outcome, Islamabad has been investing significant time and resources to the success of the mediation efforts. The outcome has been far from assured.
Some see this as another example of Pakistan over-promising and falling short of delivering. But there’s a bigger question behind recent events: Why does every revival of Pakistan-U.S. relations require another geopolitical crisis?
The problem is that Pakistan-U.S. relations lack enough independent commercial, institutional, academic, and professional connections to maintain political engagement when the immediate geopolitical transaction ends. 
The contrast with India-U.S. relations helps explain this problem.
During the early 2000s, India-U.S. ties were largely driven from the top. President George W. Bush and Prime Minister Manmohan Singh pushed through the civil nuclear agreement despite serious opposition within both countries. Over the following two decades, the relationship created its own institutional and economic constituencies. Technology companies, universities, defense manufacturers, investors, and the Indian diaspora now have their own reasons for sustaining it. Daniel Markey described this as “a reversal of the motive forces behind U.S.-India ties: from top-down to bottom-up.”
This explains why India-U.S. relations have survived serious political headwinds during current U.S. President Donald Trump’s second term. The two countries disagreed over trade, immigration, Russia, Pakistan, and the war with Iran. Yet their military, economic, and technological engagement has continued. 
The clearest evidence is the new ten-year Framework for the U.S.-India Major Defense Partnership signed in October 2025 and the expansion of the Biden-era iCET (initiative on Critical and Emerging Technologies) mechanism into TRUST (Transforming Relations into Utilizing Strategic Technologies) in February 2025, covering artificial intelligence, semiconductors, quantum computing, biotechnology, energy, space, critical minerals, and pharmaceutical supply chains. 
When it comes to China, the Trump administration’s narrower focus on denying Beijing control of the First Island Chain arguably reduces India’s direct operational relevance compared with Japan and the Philippines. India’s relevance in the U.S. strategic competition with China will therefore depend on whether Washington continues to see the Indian and Pacific oceans as disjointed theaters and whether India remains restricted to its immediate neighborhood.
Pakistan faces different conditions. For one, it is a close strategic and defense partner of China. Although democratic credentials are not attracting as much U.S. attention under the Trump administration, there are other constraints on the relationship. Pakistan’s security problems discourage tourism, investment, and academic exchange. Its universities and think tanks have fewer sustained partnerships with American institutions. Pakistan also lacks India’s economic scale, technological capacity, and purchasing power.
This does not mean that Pakistan lacks bottom-up ties with the United States. The United States is Pakistan’s largest single export market and one of the largest FDI sources. American companies operate profitably in sectors of Pakistan’s economy – franchising, fast-moving consumer goods, agribusiness and financial services – with growing interest in information technology, renewable energy, and healthcare. 
The Karachi-based American Business Council has more than 55 member companies, most of them Fortune 500 firms. The Lahore-based American Business Forum has 23 founding members and 22 associate members. Moreover, thousands of Pakistani healthcare professionals, STEM professionals, and academics actively bridge the economic and educational landscapes of both societies. 
Yet these connections remain demonstrably insufficient to determine the overall direction of the relationship. Political leaders, military officials, and regional events continue to provide the ballast for Pakistan-U.S..
Pakistan has apparently sought new ways to demonstrate its utility to Washington. Critical minerals, cryptocurrency, counterterrorism, and mediation with Iran all form part of this effort. While these initiatives can produce real economic and diplomatic gains, they could also reproduce the old transactional cycle if they remain agreements among senior officials or a small number of political- and military-linked businesses.
It is difficult for Pakistan to reproduce India’s bottom-up relationship with the United States, given India’s relative economic scale and its geopolitical position vis-à-vis China. 
Still, Islamabad can become less dependent on its temporary geopolitical utility. This would require producing high value-added textile exports and diversifying the overall export supplies. Pakistan can also do more to attract U.S. grassroots engagement by improving domestic security, ensuring constant energy supply, sustaining the current simplified tariff and tax regime to attract investment, protecting contracts and intellectual property, and building stronger links among universities, think tanks, and businesses. 
Pakistan should also use its diaspora for professional, technological, and commercial cooperation instead of viewing it mainly as a source of remittances and political support.
Pursuing these policies will ensure Pakistan-U.S. integration beyond just economic diplomacy. Instead of announcing deals and foreign visits to catch ephemeral attention, Islamabad must commit toward building industries and relationships with the U.S. that continue after the leaders leave office or the geopolitical focus shifts. Doing so will give the partnership a stronger foundation.
Twenty-five years ago, the September 11 attacks transformed Pakistan’s relationship with the United States. Almost overnight, Pakistan went from facing American sanctions and limited diplomatic attention to becoming a frontline partner in the U.S.-led war in Afghanistan.
In its counterterrorism cooperation, Pakistan offered vital ground-and air-based logistical transit to Afghanistan as well as intelligence and military action. In return, the United States provided financial reimbursement and military assistance in the form of subsidized sale of military hardware and technology. 
The relationship became increasingly strained as the two sides accused each other of failing to deliver what had been promised. Yet the two sides remained close as long as Washington needed Pakistan for the war in Afghanistan.
When the U.S. military withdrew from Afghanistan in August 2021, much of the urgency behind the relationship disappeared. Washington’s political attention declined, although counterterrorism, trade, health, and other forms of engagement continued at the institutional level.
Twenty-five years after 9/11, Pakistan and the United States appear to have entered another period of warm relations. Pakistan has again presented itself as a useful partner through mediation between Washington and Tehran, alongside cryptocurrency deals, critical mineral investments, and counterterrorism cooperation.
As Pakistan mediates in the Iran-U.S. war, given the difficulties of reaching a truce, there’s a constant fear of Pakistani leaders becoming the eventual fall guys. To avert that outcome, Islamabad has been investing significant time and resources to the success of the mediation efforts. The outcome has been far from assured.
articles.summary: There’s a reason the nation's relationship with the U.S. has fluctuated while India’s has largely held steady.

articles.title: Tashiev and the Letter of 75: Charges Reclassified, Sentences Lessened, Confusion Reigns
articles.full_text:
Both Tashiev’s lawyers and the prosecutors filed appeals after the July verdict, the former seeking complete acquittal and the latter harsher sentencing. Neither has gotten what they asked for.
When the trial of the former head of Kyrgyzstan’s State Committee for National Security, Kamchybek Tashiev, ended in July the judge delivered what appeared to be a damning verdict followed by an absurdist reprieve. 
Tashiev – alongside former Speaker of the Zhogorku Kenesh Nurlanbek Turgunbek uulu, former Member of Parliament Kurmankul Zulushev, and five others – was found guilty of a coup attempt under Article 326 (“Violent seizure or retention of power, as well as an attempt to violently change the constitutional order”) of the Kyrgyz criminal code and acquitted of abuse of office charges.
Tashiev and the rest were sentenced to four years in prison – the prosecutors had sought nine. The judge immediately replaced the prison terms with three years of supervised probation. 
Tashiev, technically convicted of a coup attempt, served not a single day in detention.
Both Tashiev’s lawyers and the prosecutors filed appeals, the former seeking complete acquittal and the latter harsher sentencing.
In early September, the Bishkek City Court heard the appeal. Like most of the first trial, the proceedings were held behind closed doors, so what happened next doesn’t have a clear explanation. The court apparently reclassified the charges from a coup attempt under Article 326 to “obstruction of the exercise of electoral rights,” Article 195. 
According to various lawyers representing the defendants, all eight were sentenced to four year prison terms, converted immediately to two years of probation.
Zhoomart Ashirbaev, the lawyer for Zulushev, told RFE/RL’s Kyrgyz Service, Azattyk, that they intended to file a cassation appeal with the Supreme Court. 
“The court’s reclassification of the charge from a serious crime to Article 195 demonstrates that the investigation brought an unfounded and unproven charge. I spoke with Kurmankul Zulushev immediately after the verdict was announced. We will file a cassation appeal to the Supreme Court.”
Latypbek Nuralimov, a lawyer representing Turgunbek uulu, told TASS, “They sentenced him to four years in prison, but they applied probation [for two years] because the crime is less serious.”
Chinara Dzhakupbekova, a lawyer representing Kursan Asanov, a former deputy minister of internal affairs charged in the case, expressed confusion over how Article 195 could even apply to the case. According to 24.kg, she said, “Article 195 can essentially only function when elections are underway. And there weren’t any elections, so this article is irrelevant.”
Kyrgyzstan isn’t due for a presidential election until January 2027.
The original trial, which started in May behind closed doors, before being briefly opened in mid-June and then closed again, centered on what’s become known as the “Letter of 75.” 
The letter – an appeal signed by 75 public figures – circulated in early February and precipitated Tashiev’s sudden ejection from the ruling tandem. The letter urged Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov to call for an early presidential election and framed Tashiev favorably, highlighting that many of the Japarov administration’s greatest successes were initiatives spearheaded by the security chief. 
During the brief period in which the trial was open, witnesses were questioned about the reception of the letter by members of parliament. The trial was closed again at the request of the defendants after Tashiev engaged in a verbal clash with a witness that included mention of the witness’s father’s 2005 murder. 
Precisely how the letter constituted, or indicated, a coup attempt is not an argument the prosecutors have made clearly in public. And now the charge has been changed entirely, from coup plot to electoral obstruction – it’s not clear why or how or who made that change. The ultimate sentences shrunk from three years probation to two.
Tashiev’s lawyer, Ikramidin Aitkulov, was rather direct with his comments to the media after the result of the appeal was announced: “Well, this is a stupid decision, frankly. Completely illegal and unfounded. Of course, we will appeal.”
