articles.title: North Korea’s Nicaragua Courtship
articles.full_text:
At a time when Pyongyang is restructuring its foreign relationships, its diplomatic focus on the Central American nation stands out.
Since emerging from its self-imposed COVID-19 isolation, North Korea has closed a number of its diplomatic missions overseas while reshaping others. The government has concentrated on relationships it sees as strategically useful, focusing heavily on deepening ties with Russia, its burgeoning relations with Belarus, and, most recently, the rekindling of engagement with China. Yet, amid this diplomatic retrenchment, one unexpected country has received particular outreach and attention from the Kim Jong Un regime: Nicaragua.
At a time when North Korea is restructuring its foreign relationships, its decision to court Nicaragua stands out, both for its geographic position and the fact that it came at the invitation of the Kim regime. While the two countries seem like natural partners given the nature of their authoritarian systems of government and long-standing history, the outreach is nevertheless a notable deviation from North Korea’s baseline behavior. Ultimately it could signal increased cooperation between the two countries as well a new trajectory for North Korea’s foreign policy designs going forward, one that exists outside China’s and Russia’s immediate orbit.
Background on the Nicaragua-North Korea relationship
North Korea’s relationship with Nicaragua has ebbed and flowed with changes in Managua’s government.
Pyongyang avoided diplomatic relations with the U.S.-backed Nicaraguan government until 1979, when the Sandinista National Liberation Front took power. At the time, the Kim regime’s connections to the Sandinistas largely ran through its Cuban partner, although North Korea had reportedly provided military training to the group’s personnel in the lead-up to the revolution.
Bilateral engagement between the two countries peaked in the 1980s. This included North Korean military assistance with the delivery of four patrol vessels valued at $8 million, as well as mutual diplomatic support. In 1986, Daniel Ortega, the Sandinista leader and then president of Nicaragua, traveled to Pyongyang for a first-of-its-kind summit between the two nations. Nicaragua followed this up with a show of solidarity by deciding to boycott the 1988 Olympics hosted in Seoul.
Bilateral ties cooled after the Sandinistas fell out of power in 1990. This eventually led to the closure of the North Korean embassy in Managua in 1995. 
It was not until Ortega returned to power in 2006 that the two governments reestablished diplomatic relations. But it would still take another decade before the next notable development.
In January 2017, a North Korean delegation headed by Choe Ryong Hae – one of Kim Jong Un’s top officials – attended the inauguration of Daniel Ortega for his third term as president of Nicaragua. There, the two governments lauded nearly 40 years of friendship and mutual diplomatic support.
However, the practical depth of the relationship remained shallow. In 2017, North Korea’s exports to Nicaragua were reportedly worth just $1.8 million, while reciprocal trade was minimal. There were no indications of military cooperation, and diplomatic engagement remained surface-level. Beyond the ceremonial nature of Choe Ryong Hae’s visit, there was little indication that the relationship was poised to deepen.
The COVID-19 pandemic marked a substantial turning point for North Korean foreign relations. The border lockdowns and restrictions on movement of overseas personnel sharply curtailed diplomatic activities. All but a handful of embassies in Pyongyang closed owing to movement restrictions and resource depletion, reducing contact between foreign diplomats and North Korea government officials.
This self-imposed isolation enabled the Kim regime to reset its policy designs going forward. The Eighth Party Congress in January 2021 produced a five-year policy roadmap for North Korea. The implications for foreign policy began to manifest when emerging from the COVID-19 lockdown period.
As North Korea began reopening in 2023, evidence of this restructuring of foreign partnerships became increasingly visible. Pyongyang closed its embassies in Angola (2023), Bangladesh (2023), Democratic Republic of the Congo (2023), Guinea (2023), Libya (2024), Nepal (2023), Senegal (2023), Spain (2023), Syria (2024), and Uganda (2023).
Although North Korea’s government did not give a specific reason for these closures, it signaled a reallocation of resources that went toward other relationships it wished to cultivate further. North Korea opened additional consulates in Russia, pursued deeper engagement with Belarus – culminating with Alexander Lukashenko’s March 2026 visit – and, curiously, invited Nicaragua to open an embassy in Pyongyang.
In July 2023, the Kim regime sent a delegation to Nicaragua to propose that Managua set up an embassy in the North Korean capital. Pyongyang’s state media did not publicize the initiative; rather, it was the Nicaraguan government that revealed the invitation. Within a year, Managua had inaugurated its diplomatic mission in Pyongyang and presented ambassadorial credentials to the North Korean government.
Since then, North Korea has increasingly referenced Nicaragua in its state media reporting. In the official news wire service, KCNA, Nicaragua has been the subject of 12 reports so far in 2026, after 15 in 2025 and eight in 2024. This compares to only two in 2023.
There are still unanswered questions as to why Pyongyang extended this outreach. Does North Korea see potential for trade (arms or otherwise)? Is Pyongyang seeking to expand its own work in the region?
Part of the answer may lie in Cuba, a longtime partner of both governments. At the same time that North Korea was seeking to advance ties with the Nicaraguan government, South Korea was moving to normalize diplomatic relations with Cuba. Cuba had long maintained close ties with the North while keeping its distance from South Korea, but that changed in February 2024 when Havana and Seoul formalized ties.
This move was a diplomatic setback for Pyongyang, which had up to that point maintained its third-largest embassy in Havana (behind Moscow and Beijing). In essence, Seoul’s encroachment in Cuba marked the potential weakening of a key regional partnership for the Kim regime.
Notably, Nicaragua closed its embassy in South Korea in April 2024. Although Managua cited budget constraints as its reason for the closure, the timing was notable: it came just two months after the Cuba-South Korea normalization of relations and amid Pyongyang’s continued courtship of Nicaragua. Whether the events were connected, however, remains unclear.
But finding a regional partner is only part of the equation. Other Central American countries maintain friendly relations with North Korea, raising the question of what makes Nicaragua stand out for Pyongyang.
In practice, North Korea’s preferred relationships have been with those countries that satisfy three prerequisites. First, they are looser in their adherence to the rules-based international order. Second, they are not closely aligned with the United States, South Korea, or their allies and partners. Third, the country lacks something that North Korea can provide, giving Pyongyang a potential source of leverage. 
Nicaragua satisfies those three criteria. The United States strongly opposes the Sandinista government, and Nicaragua no longer maintains a diplomatic mission in Seoul. Further, Nicaragua’s traditional security relationships with Cuba and Venezuela have become less reliable, creating potential space for another source of military equipment or training.
From Managua’s perspective, North Korea offers a like-minded partner with a similarly personalized, family-centric political system. This is in part why Nicaragua has earned the moniker the “North Korea of Latin America.” 
For governments run by families like the Ortega-Murillo regime, North Korea offers an example of how an under-resourced authoritarian government can survive sustained pressure from much larger powers. This only reinforces the legacy of extremes that Nicaragua has faced under both the Ortega-Murillo government and the Somoza government that preceded it. Authoritarianism has been the dominant force in Nicaragua for most of its political history, and North Korea offers a useful example both to tout and follow.
But the similarity between systems of government is only a starting point for solidarity, as there are practical considerations as well. The relationship can also facilitate cooperation when other economic and security channels become constrained by international pressure. For a regime that prioritizes survival, North Korea offers capabilities that may matter despite the country’s relatively small economic footprint. Pyongyang has decades of experience operating under sanctions and maintaining security relationships with similarly isolated governments.
These capabilities may expand into the military realm. For years, Russia has been the principal supplier of arms and training to the Nicaraguan military, but Managua has recently signed agreements with Beijing to deepen China-Nicaragua security ties. North Korea provides another potential source of equipment and know-how for the Ortega-Murillo regime.
For all the diplomatic activity, tangible economic and security cooperation still remains limited. For example, the primary recorded exports for the two countries in 2024 were rolled tobacco from Nicaragua and delivery trucks from North Korea. 
That could change as Russian demand for North Korean equipment and personnel necessary for the Russia-Ukraine War draws down.
articles.summary: At a time when Pyongyang is restructuring its foreign relationships, its diplomatic focus on the Central American nation stands out.

articles.title: Shifting Poles and Power 35 Years After the End of the Soviet Union
articles.full_text:
For many post-Soviet states, multipolarity is nothing new. Navigating between competing powers has been an important part of their security strategy since independence.
Since late August, seven of the 15 republics of the former Soviet Union celebrated the 35th anniversary of the declaration of their independence. Some marked the occasion in spectacular fashion, such as Uzbekistan and others with more sedate celebrations. But all sought to display and embrace the national identities they have developed since attaining sovereignty. 
In 1991, the Soviet Union collapsed and the bipolar world of the time came to an end. In the post-Cold War period, widely described as a period of U.S. unipolarity, when there was no power that could seriously challenge U.S. supremacy, the new republics worked hard to strengthen their national identities. 
The rise of China, and Russia’s resurgence under President Vladimir Putin, changed the balance of power in the late 2000s. 
Today, the dominant narrative – not only in countries of the Global South in general and in the post-Soviet space in particular but increasingly in Western discourse, too – is that the world is shifting toward a different system, a multipolar one. 
This multipolarity is on display across the post-Soviet space. The Baltic states, for example, became NATO members in the early 2000s. In Eastern Europe, while Belarus became a close ally of Russia, Ukraine hedged and then inched toward the West. In Russian discourse, Ukraine’s desire to join NATO was a threat to Moscow’s security. Other states in the South Caucasus and Central Asia continue to hedge among the various poles in the emerging multipolar world. 
What does security look like for the current post-Soviet states? Has the world indeed become multipolar for these states or has it been multipolar for them all along? There is a plethora of alliances, blocs, and various other groups in the world today, many which border or reach into the post-Soviet space: From the Western-led NATO, to BRICS, the Shanghai Cooperation Organization, and the Collective Security Treaty Organization, each built around the perceived national interests of states, their history and power politics in the region. More recently, one could argue, such groups have formed around religious identity, such as the Mecca Pact involving Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, and Türkiye. The world is transitioning toward an international system with several centers of power. Whether we call it a multipolar world or something else, the emergence of different poles seems clear.
In the post-Soviet space, over the past three decades, these poles have largely been centered around Russia, China, and the United States. Chinese expansion in the region has reached unprecedented levels in particular. China has replaced Russia as the main trading partner of most of the Central Asian states. While Russia has pursued an alternative Eurasian security order in the post-Soviet space, China’s economic power and the scale of its economic engagement have made it increasingly dominant through its geoeconomic programs, including the Belt and Road Initiative and other credit and assistance schemes. 
Until Russia’s war in Ukraine, security and international relations scholars were broadly discussing and researching how interstate war had declined since the Second World War, with more casualties coming from civil wars and domestic unrest. 
In my security and international relations classes, we mostly focused on internal conflicts, conflicts involving non-state actors, and terrorism. This thinking changed in 2022, when Russia invaded Ukraine, followed by Israel’s war in Gaza in 2023 and, more recently, the U.S. war in Iran. None of these active wars appears to be ending soon. Multiple conflicts and ongoing Cold War-like rivalries indicate that there are several powers fighting for what they believe is their sphere of influence.
While countries in the Global South have been talking about multipolarity for some time, it was only after U.S. President Donald Trump’s shift towards a more isolationist foreign policy for the U.S., as well as his demands for NATO members to look after their own security, that the topic of multiple poles and spheres of influence has became more serious.  This was reinforced by the Canadian prime minister’s reference to the importance of middle powers working together in the new world, presented in a speech to the World Economic Forum in Davos in January. The transition toward multiple spheres of influence is accompanied by a shift toward nationalist and isolationist policies.
More recently, Türkiye has emerged as a new pole for the Central Asian states. Four Central Asian states share a common Turkic identity. Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan ,and Türkiye are members of the Organization of Turkic States (OTS), which brings these countries together around their Turkic identity, while Turkmenistan is an observer. It is perhaps the first organization that unites these states based on their local Turkic languages and culture rather than the prior regional lingua franca, Russian. 
It is hard to say if we are now in a fully multipolar world or whether it has always been so for the states in the post-Soviet space. Nationalist tendencies are on the rise in many societies today, for example the rise of Reform U.K. in the United Kingdom, the recent victory of Germany’s far-right AfD, and the growing influence of One Nation in Australia. In this changing global system, we see not only an ideological dimension, reflected in the Western and non-Western divide, but also an identity-driven dimension, as illustrated by the recent Mecca Pact and the OTS. For many states in Central Asia, it remains important to maximize their national interests while coexisting with multiple poles competing for influence in the region – something that has always been the case.

articles.title: North Korean Elites and Regime Weakness
articles.full_text:
North Koreans pay their respects before the 20 meter tall Kim Il Sung and Kim Jong Il statues at the center of the Mansu Hill Grand Monument located at Mansudae, Pyongyang, North Korea.
The Diplomat author Mercy Kuo regularly engages subject-matter experts, policy practitioners, and strategic thinkers across the globe for their diverse insights into U.S. Asia policy.  This conversation with Dr. Jieun Baek – author of “Privileged but Powerless: How North Korean Elite Grievances Reveal the Regime’s Greatest Weakness” (Yale 2026) – is the 525th in “The Trans-Pacific View Insight Series.”
Describe the key characteristics of North Korea’s elites.
North Korea officially rejects the idea that it has an elite class, yet it is one of the world’s most stratified societies. Its elites include Korean Workers’ Party cadres, intellectuals, senior military and security officials, and individuals personally close to Kim Jong Un. The traditional elite largely inherits status through favorable songbun [North Korea’s hierarchical classification system], family history, and proven political loyalty. A newer unofficial elite – the donju, or “masters of money” – derives influence from capital, markets, and connections.
These groups are not monolithic, but they share one defining characteristic: their positions help maintain the regime. In return, they may receive Pyongyang residency, superior housing and education, better food, prestigious employment and education, overseas opportunities, and access to luxury goods – European watches, imported cosmetics, pet poodles. 
None of this is discreet. The regime stages elite reward deliberately. When the Kyongru-dong neighborhood opened, officials framed the new housing not as a public good but as the deserved inheritance of those whose loyalty had earned them “the best of civilization.”
Yet every privilege is conditional. Elites must continuously demonstrate political reliability, professional usefulness, and personal loyalty to Kim. And the most privileged are also the most closely watched: privilege and surveillance rise together.
Examine why North Korean elites are “privileged but powerless.”
North Korean elites possess influence, wealth, and access unimaginable to most citizens, but they lack the most basic power over their own lives. They cannot safely criticize policy, organize independently, protect their families from guilt by association, or know whether today’s privilege will survive tomorrow’s purge. Even the most senior officials can be demoted, imprisoned, or executed without due process, like Jang Song Thaek in 2013.
Their proximity to power actually creates additional danger. Elites face intense surveillance, mandatory ideological activity, extractive “loyalty” contributions, workplace rivalries, and constant evaluation. Thae Yong Ho, the most senior North Korean diplomat to defect in years, put it with characteristic economy: “The closer you are to the Sun, the higher the chances you will burn.” Several escapees told me middle-ranking posts felt safer than the apex.
They may supervise institutions or control substantial resources, but they cannot challenge the system that grants those privileges. As one elite escapee told me, they are “disposable slaves to Kim Jong Un.” They are powerful downward, toward those beneath them, but powerless upward, before the Leader.
Analyze the correlation between North Korean elite “feigned fealty” and the erosion of elite loyalty to Kim Jong Un’s regime.
North Korean public life is a carefully directed performance. Elites attend rallies, recite ideological texts, participate in self-criticism sessions, and display intense devotion. But visible obedience should not be mistaken for sincere belief.
One interviewee described this perfectly through an anecdote. Inspectors would arrive at his home in white gloves to check the portraits of the Kim leaders, hunting for a speck of dust that could bring serious consequences down on his family. He cleaned those portraits, he told me, not out of reverence but out of self-preservation.
As depicted in the table below, “Feigned fealty” describes that widening gap between low inward loyalty and high outward loyalty. Many elites perform devotion because doing so protects their careers, families, status, and lives. This is preference falsification under extreme coercion: everyone plays a role, while few can know what others truly believe.
The gap appears to be widening under Kim Jong Un. Elite defections have increased dramatically; younger elites prioritize money, business, foreign study, and opportunities for their children over service to the Party; and many privately favor economic reform and greater access to information. The regime’s elaborate demands for loyalty reveal not confidence, but anxiety. A system sustained by genuine conviction is resilient. One sustained by surveillance, rewards, and fear may look stable until a shock exposes how shallow its support has become.
Identify the five options for North Korean elites with grievances.
Aggrieved elites have five primary options.
First, they can maintain the status quo and do nothing. This is the least immediately dangerous and most rational choice, but it allows resentment and distrust to accumulate beneath the surface.
Second, they can defect and seek asylum abroad. Defection is an unequivocal rejection of the regime, but it carries extraordinary risks for escapees and their families.
Third, they can erode the regime’s monopoly over resources by building alternative power structures. Markets, private food production, solar energy, informal finance, tutoring, communications, housing, and healthcare can gradually reduce dependence on the state.
Fourth, they can engage in dissent – from coded criticism and hidden transcripts, to use James C. Scott’s concept, and subtle defiance to clandestine information sharing or organized resistance.
Fifth, they can push for democratization and systemic reform. This is the most ambitious and dangerous option because it requires trust, coordination, and first movers willing to confront enormous barriers to collective action.
Assess the role of North Korean elite grievances in revealing the regime’s greatest weakness and its implications for U.S., European, and Asian policymakers and geopolitical strategists.
The regime’s greatest strength and greatest weakness are the same: its dependence on elites. Elites are its architects, administrators, financiers, enforcers, and protectors. The broader population can be controlled through isolation and terror, but the regime must continuously manage elites through a delicate combination of privilege, surveillance, and coercion. If elite allegiance fractures, the system’s foundation begins to crack.
Policymakers should therefore look beyond missile tests and leadership imagery to study elite incentives, generational change, defections, market activity, information consumption, and signs of preference falsification. They should avoid assuming that elite dissatisfaction will automatically produce reform; North Korea’s barriers to trust and collective action remain formidable.
They should also avoid inadvertently improving the regime’s capacity to reward loyalty. Hard-currency access, prestige projects, and engagement channels the state can capture are redirected into patronage for insiders. Sanctions design and diplomatic sweeteners deserve to be tested against that standard.
The United States, Europe, South Korea, Japan, and other partners should expand secure access to outside information, combining radio and portable media with technologies that circumvent censorship. North Korean escapees should lead content creation so that it is credible, tailored, and safe for intended audiences. Governments should also protect escapees, strengthen pathways for asylum, document elite testimony, and support decentralized economic and information networks that reduce the state’s monopoly over daily life.
Finally, strategists must prepare for multiple futures, including gradual liberalization, elite-led reform, succession instability, or sudden internal shock. North Korea may appear immovable, but a regime that requires constant performances of loyalty is revealing its fear: that when people are finally free to choose, many of its most privileged citizens may choose something else.

articles.summary: Insights from Jieun Baek.

articles.title: The Ultimate Hedger: Why Vietnam Is Thriving Amid Global Disorder
articles.full_text:
Vietnam is deeply committed, for strategic and historic reasons, to respond to uncertainty and global geopolitical tensions by hedging. And it’s working.
To Lam, general secretary of the Central Committee of the Communist Party of Vietnam and president of Vietnam, delivered the Keynote Address at the 23rd IISS Shangri-La Dialogue, May 29, 2026.
Vietnam has emerged as a leading strategic hedger in a global order undergoing major power transition. In other words, it has engaged in “repeated, diverse, sustained, and complementary actions to engage with all major powers without reaching a formal alliance with any and without restrictions on possible actions with others.”
On April 2, 2025, Vietnam’s strategy faced a massive test: on so-called “Liberation Day,” U.S. President Donald Trump targeted Vietnam with a punishing 46 percent tariff, accusing the country of conniving with China on transshipment and treating the United States unfairly. Totaling $123.5 billion, the U.S. trade deficit with Vietnam was the third largest after its deficits with China and Mexico. It attracted attention. 
On April 14-15, Chinese President Xi Jinping was in Hanoi, pressuring Vietnam not to give in too much to the United States. With pressure from both sides, the future of Vietnam as a connector country in global supply chains was under great stress.
Fast forward 16 months, and Vietnam has not just survived in the disorder; it has thrived. 
Overall exports increased by 17 percent in 2025 overall (and exports to the U.S. increased 28 percent, to $153 billion). In the first seven months of 2026, the U.S. imported $104.7 billion worth of goods from Vietnam, a 23 percent year-on-year increase. Vietnam’s GDP growth rate reached 8 percent in 2025 and 8.18 percent in the first half of 2026, despite trade tensions and the Iran war, and in contrast to the prediction of 5.6 percent for 2025 made by the IMF Outlook in September 2025. 
To accomplish this economic feat, Vietnam did not throw its lot in with one great power or join an alliance. In fact, it doubled down in its strategic behavior as a hedger. Vietnam is deeply committed, for strategic and historic reasons, to respond to uncertainty and global geopolitical tensions by hedging.
Amazingly, it has worked so far. Vietnam seems particularly able to succeed in hedging and resist the formidable pressures of three great powers – not only China and the U.S., but Russia – due to three key advantages. First, Vietnam’s crucial geopolitical position means that no great power can let another dominate, forcing them to show some forbearance. 
Second, Vietnam has built a position of structural indispensability in supply chains as the recipient of investments linked to businesses’ “China plus one” or out-of-China strategy. For many Western firms, Vietnam is hard to replace. Vietnam has also started to diversify its markets. 
Third, Vietnam has shown tactical genius in handling each of the three great powers and their leaders.
With the United States, Vietnam negotiated intensely and directly, the day after the tariffs were announced. Getting ahead of ASEAN solidarity, it engaged intensely with Washington and on July 2, 2025, became the third country to reach a deal with the Trump administration, after the United Kingdom and China. The deal reduced U.S. tariffs to 20 percent (and 40 percent on transshipments, although the term is not well defined) and committed Vietnam to across-the-board opening to U.S. exports. These conditions were reconfirmed in a formal White House Fact Sheet in October. But, crucially, Vietnam refused to accept poison pill restrictions and commitments to follow U.S. sanctions on China, unlike Malaysia and Cambodia at the time. 
Even the lowered tariffs led to painful supply chain adjustments and automation, but Vietnam’s efforts mitigated the worst of the damage.
At the same time, Vietnam went out of its way to signal opening to Trump’s own priorities. In May 2025, the Ministry of Finance led the largest-ever Vietnamese corporate delegation to the Select USA fair in Maryland. They enlisted some U.S. corporate support in fending off further tariffs. The same month, on May 16-21, Vietnam fast-tracked a $1.5 billion real estate investment by the Trump Organization, with events attended by Eric Trump. 
On February 18-20, 2026, Secretary General of the Communist Party of Vietnam To Lam traveled to the United States to attend the opening ceremony of the Trump Board of Peace for Gaza and sign a flurry of cooperation agreements.
Yet, Vietnam would not cross certain boundaries with the U.S. Hanoi’s willingness to compromise did not prevent a strong push to resume the war legacy remediation program, which had been disrupted by the dismantlement of USAID. The United States gave in – Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth came to Hanoi and committed another $130 million to the fund, but he could not persuade Vietnam to sign an arms deal. Vietnam also refused to take measures that would antagonize China or Russia and refused to join the Pax Silica initiative.
At the same time, Vietnam underwent intensified engagement with China. As mentioned earlier, Chinese leader Xi Jinping visited Hanoi in April 2025 and Vietnamese leader To Lam reciprocated with a visit to Beijing on April 14-17, 2026, leading to the conclusion of a joint statement and 32 cooperation agreements. Foreign ministers also visited each other, as well as Vietnam’s former prime minister and president. The increased cooperation resulted in new MOUs between Chinese and Vietnamese media that include content co-production terms and the promotion of people-to-people ties. In terms of sheer number of agreements, Vietnam signed more with China than the United States over the past year and half.
On AI governance, Minister Vu Hai Quan led a delegation to the Shanghai World AI Conference, butinitially refused to join the 29 founding members of the World AI Cooperation Organization (WAICO) created by China, unlike Indonesia and Malaysia. Here again, Vietnam kept to its hedging playbook, apparently refusing to cross a U.S. red line. However, on July 31, Vietnam ended up joining WAICO in a low-key manner, along with seven other new members. But the Vietnam scholarly community does not interpret this as a making a choice between Pax Silica and WAICO.
Vietnam similarly intensified its long relationship with Russia. No fewer than seven Vietnamese leaders have visited Russia since January 2025, including top leader To Lam on May 9-12, 2025. During that visit, the two leaders signed a major joint statement that accelerated energy cooperation. In March 2026, Vietnam reached a nuclear deal with Rosatom to fast-track the building of one nuclear reactor in Khan Hoa province, leaving Japanese, French, Korean, and U.S. companies disappointed. Vietnam and Russia regularly discuss maritime issues, with General Phan Van Giang’s visit to Moscow in May 2025 offering Vietnam some support in the South China Sea.
Over the past 18 months, Vietnam also upgraded and intensified its relations and economic engagement with Japan, India, South Korea, Australia, New Zealand, the U.K., France, and the EU. In fact, since January 2025, Vietnam has deepened its strategic partnerships with existing partners, while adding six comprehensive strategic partners (the U.K., the EU, Indonesia, New Zealand, Singapore, and Thailand), nine new strategic partners, and two new comprehensive partners.
In sum, Vietnam has managed so far to do well in the midst of a trade war, geopolitical tensions, and global uncertainty, all through the mastery of the art of hedging. This art is a risky one over time, with countless necessary adjustments. The question remains whether Vietnam will manage to jump all the hoops ahead.
This article has been updated to note Vietnam’s membership in WAICO.

articles.title: Russia Is Helping Supercharge North Korea’s Military Drones
articles.full_text:
North Korea, already receiving Russian drone technology, could eventually gain access to more advanced capabilities like autonomous AI‑enabled and jet‑powered drones.
In this photo provided by North Korean state media, North Korean leader Kim Jong Un attends tests of “various kinds of reconnaissance and suicide drones” developed and produced by the Unmanned Aerial Technology Alliance, Mar. 18, 2025.
Russia’s expanding military partnership with North Korea has become one of the most significant proliferation risks of the Ukraine war. Since Pyongyang began actively supporting Russia’s campaign, Moscow is believed to have transferred sensitive technologies such as naval reactors for nuclear‑powered submarines, air defense systems, and other advanced capabilities in exchange for North Korean weapons and troops. Russia has already provided drone technology to Pyongyang, and the rapid evolution of Russian battlefield innovations now raises concerns that North Korea could, in time, gain access to far more sophisticated systems, including new versions of autonomous AI–enabled and jet–powered drones.
In a war that began as an artillery‑heavy conflict, drone usage and tactics have evolved rapidly. One of the most consequential developments is Russia’s experimentation with autonomously controlled AI‑enabled drones. Earlier iterations required a human operator to confirm targets, with AI used primarily to counter radio‑jamming and ensure the drone reached its destination. In recent months, however, Russia has begun allowing onboard AI systems to make independent strike decisions. This shift toward autonomous targeting represents a significant technological leap and raises concerns that North Korea, already receiving Russian drone technology, could eventually gain access to these more advanced capabilities.
As with much of the evolution of technology in the Ukraine war, Russia’s has equipped its autonomous AI drones with off-the-shelf technology, specifically commercial grade Nvidia Jetson Orin computers designed to create AI-enabled devices. Using such tools, Russia is training the drone AI to identify specific targets such as gas stations.
Russia has also begun modifying drones with jet powered engines. Jet powered drones are more expensive than the propellor powered models that have been heavily utilized during the war, but they are also more difficult to shoot down. The Geran-5, a Russian version of the Shahed drone, also has a China connection: Its 200 kilogram-thrust turbojet engines are believed to have Chinese origins.
North Korean Drone Cooperation With Russia
Since becoming active in the war against Ukraine, North Korea has transferred over 15 million artillery shells and provided Russia with an estimated 15,000 troops. Reports suggest that Moscow agreed to provide drone technology to Pyongyang in exchange for the troop deployment, but North Korea’s decision to provide Russia with cluster bombs for its suicide drones was likely also a factor. 
The partnership that has developed between Russia and North Korea has allowed Pyongyang to rapidly advance its drone development program. Prior to the Ukraine war, North Korea only possessed outdated reconnaissance drone technology despite development efforts dating back at least to the early 2010s, including initial efforts to develop a strike drone based on U.S. technology. The war in Ukraine, however, has allowed Pyongyang to not only undertake rapid technological advances in its drone technology but to also gain battlefield experience in utilizing them.
When Russian President Vladimir Putin met North Korean leader Kim Jong Un in September 2023, Russia provided North Korea with four suicide drones and one reconnaissance drone. More significantly, Russia is believed to have transferred the technology behind Iran’s Shahed-136 drone, the template for Russian drone advances, to North Korea, as well as equipment to enable production. 
North Korea has also unveiled its Geumseong series tactical attack drones, which closely resemble Russia’s Lancet‑3 loitering munition and Israel’s HERO‑30, a similarity that strongly suggests additional technology transfers from Moscow. Pyongyang claims the Geumseong series is already AI–enabled, a capability it has not previously demonstrated. Given North Korea’s limited domestic experience with autonomous guidance systems and Russia’s active development of AI‑driven loitering munitions, this initial integration of AI was almost certainly achieved with Russian assistance.
Pyongyang has additionally benefited from its partnership with Russia beyond the transfer of technology. Unconfirmed reports suggest that North Korean laborers were being recruited through the Jihyang Technology Trading Company to support production of Shahed/Geran drones at Russia’s Yelabuga drone production facility in Tartistan. The North Korean workers were expected to assist in production and handle secondary and itinerary assembly, practical skills that would over time enhance North Korea’s own ability to produce drones.
North Korean troops have also gained practical tactical experience in drone warfare on the battlefield. North Korean tactics quickly evolved during their deployment to Russia to the realities of drone warfare. This includes the deployment of troops in smaller groups to evade enemy drones and adoption of tactics in long-range strike missions. 
Pyongyang’s participation in the war is also giving it access to real world data on the success of North Korean drones and ballistic missiles against Western defensive systems, and access to Russian operational tactics for electronic warfare. Taken together the knowledge gained from North Korea’s combat experience will enhance its ability to utilize drones and evade defensive systems.
Will North Korea Produce AI-Enabled or Jet-Powered Drones?
In 2025, the General Staff Department ordered the North Korean military to integrate AI into both manned and unmanned systems, including drones. With AI integration part of North Korea’s weapons development policy, advances in the field from Russia are likely to be adopted in time. 
The Jetson Orin computers in Russian drones are commercial grade parts and had circuit boards printed with “Made in China.” Russia is likely procuring them from illicit Chinese supply chains; North Korea will be able to as well. The kits are also relatively cheap. Some versions cost less than $300. 
Given the battlefield experience that North Korea has gained in Russia using drones and the technology cooperation between the two, including initial usage of AI, it would seem only a matter of time before Pyongyang integrated autonomous AI strike drones into its arsenal. This will enhance its ability to hit targets in the South, including civilian infrastructure, and overwhelm traditional missile defense systems over time. 
Jet powered drones would require North Korea to make modifications to its production lines that go beyond those needed for AI adoption or other iterative advances drone technology from the war. While Pyongyang could likely acquire the engines from China or develop its own version, doing so would raise the cost of its drones but not to an extent that it would be prohibitive using off-the-shelf technology.
Strategic Challenges for the United States and South Korea
As Russia continues to push the boundaries of drone technology, we should expect those innovations to make their way to North Korea with implications for security on the Korean Peninsula. Notably, South Korea’s own drone technology, especially drone interceptors, is still in an early stage of development. 
In the current conflict, the use of drones in combination with traditional ballistic missiles has overwhelmed missile defense systems with sustained attacks. Drones are both cheaper and more easily produced than ballistic missile interceptors. They also have rendered tanks useless and hindered the advance of ground troops. Because these systems are highly mobile and easy to hide, they are difficult for even militaries with air superiority to eliminate, as the Iran-U.S. war has demonstrated. 
Autonomous targeting drones and jet-powered drones will provide North Korea with increasingly capable asymmetric tools to counter the United States and South Korea during a conflict. While they will not provide North Korea with a decisive advantage, they will complicate allied operations and increase the cost to civilian infrastructure and military systems that will be required to win a conflict.
This shift to cheaper, more mobile, and increasingly autonomous systems is a trend that will reshape conflict for the foreseeable future and one that the United States and South Korea must adapt to more quickly.
Russia’s expanding military partnership with North Korea has become one of the most significant proliferation risks of the Ukraine war. Since Pyongyang began actively supporting Russia’s campaign, Moscow is believed to have transferred sensitive technologies such as naval reactors for nuclear‑powered submarines, air defense systems, and other advanced capabilities in exchange for North Korean weapons and troops. Russia has already provided drone technology to Pyongyang, and the rapid evolution of Russian battlefield innovations now raises concerns that North Korea could, in time, gain access to far more sophisticated systems, including new versions of autonomous AI–enabled and jet–powered drones.
In a war that began as an artillery‑heavy conflict, drone usage and tactics have evolved rapidly. One of the most consequential developments is Russia’s experimentation with autonomously controlled AI‑enabled drones. Earlier iterations required a human operator to confirm targets, with AI used primarily to counter radio‑jamming and ensure the drone reached its destination. In recent months, however, Russia has begun allowing onboard AI systems to make independent strike decisions. This shift toward autonomous targeting represents a significant technological leap and raises concerns that North Korea, already receiving Russian drone technology, could eventually gain access to these more advanced capabilities.
As with much of the evolution of technology in the Ukraine war, Russia’s has equipped its autonomous AI drones with off-the-shelf technology, specifically commercial grade Nvidia Jetson Orin computers designed to create AI-enabled devices. Using such tools, Russia is training the drone AI to identify specific targets such as gas stations.
Russia has also begun modifying drones with jet powered engines. Jet powered drones are more expensive than the propellor powered models that have been heavily utilized during the war, but they are also more difficult to shoot down. The Geran-5, a Russian version of the Shahed drone, also has a China connection: Its 200 kilogram-thrust turbojet engines are believed to have Chinese origins.
North Korean Drone Cooperation With Russia
Since becoming active in the war against Ukraine, North Korea has transferred over 15 million artillery shells and provided Russia with an estimated 15,000 troops. Reports suggest that Moscow agreed to provide drone technology to Pyongyang in exchange for the troop deployment, but North Korea’s decision to provide Russia with cluster bombs for its suicide drones was likely also a factor.
articles.summary: North Korea, already receiving Russian drone technology, could eventually gain access to more advanced capabilities like autonomous AI‑enabled and jet‑powered drones.

articles.title: Which Document Proves Indian Citizenship? There Isn’t 1 Answer
articles.full_text:
Indian laws never specified any single document as proof of citizenship, but the Modi government’s citizenship screening drive has turned it into a big question.
In August 2026, two former Indian bureaucrats faced a challenge they never expected: they were asked to prove their Indian citizenship.
Navdeep Suri was India’s ambassador to the UAE and Egypt, while Ramesh Chander had served as ambassador to Belarus, among their other assignments. However, amid the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of the electoral roll, their names were missing from the 2003 voter list, which is being considered as the baseline of the last “pure roll.”
Their names are missing from the 2003 roll because they were serving India abroad at that time. But the voter roll revision mechanism flagged them as suspected doubtful citizens. They were told that ordinary identity documents like Aadhaar and Voter ID will not do; they will have to support their claim with more solid documents like passports, birth certificates or old land records.
The government has said the ongoing SIR is nothing but a routine electoral roll revision process, but in a country where no single document serves as proof of citizenship — and citizenship is essential for voting rights — the electoral roll revision has led to a rush for a range of documents, from birth and school-leaving certificates to land records.
Many applied for passports even though they have no plan for travelling abroad, only because they considered a passport to be unquestionable proof of citizenship.
However, a Ministry of External Affairs official said in June that an Indian passport is a “travel document” and not itself a document of Indian citizenship and that it had never been regarded as conclusive proof of citizenship.
Others have contested this claim, citing how the government’s own material on Overseas Citizens of India (OCI) says that an Indian passport is given only to an Indian citizen.
In any case, only about 7 percent of India’s population currently holds a passport, meaning the very document many now treat as the gold standard is one most citizens have never needed and don’t have.
As recent statements by different ministers and government officials, as well as court rulings, reveal, there is no single document that alone can prove one’s Indian citizenship. It is not an issue as long as one’s citizenship is not challenged. However, as soon as one’s citizenship is challenged, the burden of proof lies on that person.
The Citizenship Act recognizes citizenship principally through birth, descent, registration, naturalization and incorporation of territory. People belonging to the last three categories usually have citizenship certificates. However, for people belonging to the first two categories — who form the overwhelming majority of Indians — citizenship has to be proved through other documents.
According to a Q & A on a government website, “citizenship can be proved by any documents related to date and place of birth.” The government has not yet clearly notified any specific document. However, it has repeatedly rejected common identity documents like Aadhaar, PAN (tax ID), voter ID, driving license, ration cards and bank records as proof of citizenship.
Recently, a Calcutta High Court ruling said that possession of a voter card, Aadhaar card, bank account documents and PAN card does not automatically constitute conclusive proof of Indian citizenship.
A Guwahati High Court order in 2022 had echoed a similar view:  there is not a single document that can prove the citizenship of a person. Documents, including passport, ration card and voter ID, can constitute supporting evidence, but citizenship had to be assessed from the totality of evidence.
Recent government policies indicate that the government is increasing emphasis on birth certificates; they are being made mandatory in several aspects like admission in educational institutes and for driving licenses. The Union government has tightened rules for delayed registration of birth certificates, prioritizing integrity of the document for its importance in official purposes, including identity and citizenship-related documentation.
Over the past year and a half, when thousands, mostly Bengali-speaking Muslims, were detained in different states as suspected illegal Bangladeshi migrants, the police had mostly insisted on passports, birth certificates or school leaving certificates
The citizenship screening drive to ensure a voter roll free from illegal foreigners has led to problems due to multiple factors. Many people, especially of an older generation and from the marginalized sections of society, do not possess land records, birth certificates or school-leaving certificates.
Birth certificate possession has risen sharply for the younger generation, but remains genuinely rare for the old. The national birth registration rate was just 56.2 percent as recently as 2000 and had reached only 84.9 percent by 2017. National Family Health Survey data shows only 26.9 percent of children under five had a birth certificate in 2005-06. As registration systems improved, this share more than doubled to 62.3 percent by 2015-16.
All this means a meaningful share of adults, particularly those born before the early 2000s, have no registered record of their own birth.
Similarly, Census 2011 data put literacy among Indians aged 60 and above at just 28 percent for women and 59 percent for men nationally. This rate is lower in rural areas.
Taken together, the electoral roll revision process imposes a heavy burden of proof on older, poorer and rural Indians — the population least likely to have the paper trail the government now demands. This is why there is widespread apprehension that the voter roll revision may end up disenfranchising millions of Indians.
Given that recent months have seen a series of deportations, including wrongful ones, the disenfranchised will have reason to feel anxious about greater harassment.

articles.title: Why the South Korea-US Alliance Needs the Dark Eagle
articles.full_text:
Focusing strictly on China’s anxieties misses a far more urgent reality: South Korea faces an existential threat from North Korea.
Soldiers with 7th Infantry Division (Multi-Domain Command – Pacific) train with the Dark Eagle Long-Range Hypersonic Weapon during exercise Valiant Shield, June 6, 2026.
Rumors about the United States potentially deploying its Multi-Domain Task Force (MDTF) and the “Dark Eagle” hypersonic weapon to the Korean Peninsula are sparking predictable anxieties. Given the fierce economic and political backlash South Korea endured after hosting the Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) system in 2016, it is easy to see why critics are sounding the alarm. They argue that bringing in offensive hypersonic missiles will simply turn South Korea into a pawn in the broader China-U.S. rivalry. 
But focusing strictly on China’s anxieties and possible reaction misses a far more urgent reality: South Korea faces an existential, rapidly accelerating threat from North Korea’s evolving military capabilities.
War is no longer just fought on land, at sea, or in the air; it spills over into space, cyberspace, and the electromagnetic spectrum. The MDTF is built for this new reality. The task force is not just another conventional weapon to park on a base. It is a theater-level tool designed to blind an adversary’s radars, sever their communications, and seize control of the battlefield almost instantly.
The star of the MDTF is the Dark Eagle. According to the U.S. Army, this hypersonic glide vehicle boasts a range of over 3,500 kilometers (2,175 miles). What makes it genuinely disruptive is not just its speed – exceeding Mach 15 – but its unpredictability. Unlike traditional ballistic missiles that follow a standard, trackable arch, the Dark Eagle skims the upper atmosphere at altitudes of 30 to 50 kilometers. By flying this low and fast, it slips beneath the sightlines of ground-based early warning radars and easily bypasses legacy air defense systems.
For the Korean Peninsula, this technology rewrites the rules of deterrence. Over the past few years, North Korea has aggressively shifted toward solid-fuel ballistic missiles and mobile launchers. This means Pyongyang can roll a missile out of a tunnel and fire it in roughly 10 to 15 minutes. Older weapons, like Tomahawk cruise missiles, simply fly too slowly to eliminate these targets before they launch.
The Dark Eagle solves this timing crisis. If stationed in South Korea, it could obliterate command bunkers in Pyongyang or missile sites across the country in minutes. Even if launched from bases in Guam or Japan, the weapon would reach its target in roughly 10 minutes. This speed fundamentally shifts the strategic calculus. Knowing that a U.S. hypersonic weapon can strike the origin point of an attack almost instantly guts the logic of a surprise launch. It renders North Korea’s deeply buried nuclear bunkers highly vulnerable, serving as a visceral deterrent against miscalculation by leadership in Pyongyang.
Naturally, positioning an offensive weapon like a hypersonic missile in Northeast Asia is going to ruffle feathers. If THAAD was a shield, the Dark Eagle is undoubtedly a spear. But Seoul cannot afford to abandon the precise, asymmetric deterrence that modern weapons provide simply because of diplomatic friction with China.
Furthermore, the deployment of the MDTF would offer a strategic benefit: silencing the recurring political chatter in Washington about drawing down U.S. Forces Korea (USFK). Committing a flagship, next-generation asset to the peninsula would be ironclad proof that the United States is willing to project its most advanced military capabilities to defend South Korea.
The conversation needs to move past the rigid binary of either unconditionally hosting the MDTF forever or rejecting it out of sheer geopolitical panic. Washington and Seoul need a strategy that bolsters defense while managing diplomatic fallout. Instead of rushing into a permanent deployment, the two nations should establish a joint working group of experts and military officials to map out the logistics and political implications.
A smart first step would be a limited, rotational deployment of the MDTF during upcoming combined military exercises. This would allow both militaries to test how the Dark Eagle integrates into existing defense networks without the permanence that triggers regional crises. A phased, transparent approach buys Seoul the time it needs to build public consensus while offering diplomatic space to reassure neighbors that the weapon is meant to stabilize the region, not upend it.
Ultimately, the debate over the Dark Eagle is about much more than a single weapon system. It is a crucial test of how the U.S.-South Korea alliance is adapting to the unpredictable, multidomain threats of the 21st century. It is time approach the situation with strategic clarity, ensuring both the strength of the alliance and lasting peace on the Korean Peninsula.

articles.title: Turkish, Kazakh, and Malaysian Companies Hit With New US Sanctions Over Iran
articles.full_text:
In addition to sanctioning 27 Iranian airlines, the U.S. designated Turkish, Kazakh, and Malaysian companies for serving as general sales agents for long-sanctioned Iranian airline Mahan Air.
On September 8, the U.S. Treasury Department announced new sanctions aimed at grounding Iranian airlines, as part of the Trump administration’s “Operation Economic Outcast.” The sanctions hit 36 entities, including cargo service providers and general sales agents based in Turkiye, Kazakhstan, and Malaysia.
The Trump administration’s war against Iran has stretched into its seventh month. Although the U.S. government claims to be in control of the vital Strait of Hormuz, traffic remains low. Reuters reported that six ​commodity vessels passed through the strait on September 8, “down from ‌nine a day earlier and below the 10-day average of about 12.” In 2025, before the U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran, more than 100 commodity vessels passed through the strait each day on average.
In late August the Treasury Department announced an “economic D-Day.” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent explained: “In the Second World War, D-Day marked the historic beginning of a campaign with our allies to target and drive the enemy from its positions, including those in third countries. Today, in that same spirit, we are launching an economic onslaught against Iran’s financial connections around the globe. Our objective is to sever every economic lifeline that sustains this tyrannical regime until Tehran stands alone.”
The Treasury Department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) on September 8 designated 27 Iranian commercial airlines “for operating in the aviation sector of the Iranian economy.” 
In addition, OFAC took aim at a number of companies tied to Mahan Air, a privately owned Iranian airline. It was first sanctioned back in 2011 for providing “financial, material, and technological support to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps-Qods Force (IRGC-QF).” The Treasury Department at the time alleged that Mahan Air secretly ferried IRGC operatives, weapons, and funds. 
In 2020, OFAC designated two UAE-based companies, Parthia Cargo and Delta Parts Supply FZC, “for their material support of Iranian airline Mahan Air.” At the time, the Treasury Department outlined how the sanctioned companies helped Mahan Air “sustain its fleet of Western-manufactured aircraft.” The Treasury Department alleged that Mahan Air transported “terrorists and lethal cargo to Syria” and also “ Iranian technicians and technical equipment to Venezuela…”
In its latest round of sanctions, the Treasury Department designated several UAE-based companies it claims were involved in the transfer of three B-777 aircraft to Mahan Air.
The sanctions also designated a pair of Turkiye-based companies – S Sistem Lojistik Hizmetler Anonim Sirketi and Mes Cargo Transportation Tourism and Foreign Trade Limited Company – for coordinating shipments and serving as a general sales agent for Mahan Air. Similarly, Malaysia-based Icargo SDN BHD and Kazakhstan-based Tour Invest LLC were designated for acting as general sales agents for Mahan Air.
